docs.title: CLI flags
docs.text: yorishiro-proxy accepts command-line flags, environment variables, and a JSON config file to control its behavior. This page documents all available subcommands, flags, and the priority rules that determine which value takes effect.

docs.title: Priority order
docs.text:
When the same setting is specified in multiple places, the following priority applies:

  1. CLI flag (highest priority)
  2. Environment variable (YP_ prefix)
  3. Config file (-config)
  4. Default value (lowest priority)

docs.title: Subcommands
docs.text:
yorishiro-proxy uses a subcommand-based CLI. When no subcommand is given, it defaults to server for backward compatibility.

yorishiro-proxy [subcommand] [flags]
Subcommand Description server Start the proxy server (default when no subcommand given) client Call MCP tools via CLI against a running server docs Show tool documentation (works offline, no server needed) install Install and configure components (MCP, CA, Playwright) upgrade Check for and install updates from GitHub Releases version Print version information

docs.title: server
docs.text:
Start the proxy server. This is the default behavior when no subcommand is given.

yorishiro-proxy server [flags]
yorishiro-proxy [flags]          # equivalent — "server" is implicit

By default, the server starts an HTTP MCP transport on a random loopback port (127.0.0.1:0) and writes connection details to ~/.yorishiro-proxy/server.json for automatic client discovery.

docs.title: client
docs.text:
Call MCP tools on a running server from the command line. Useful for scripting, automation, and ad-hoc pentest workflows.

yorishiro-proxy client <tool> [key=value ...] [flags]

The client resolves the server address in this order:

  1. -server-addr flag (or YP_CLIENT_ADDR env var)
  2. -token flag (or YP_CLIENT_TOKEN env var)
  3. Auto-detection from ~/.yorishiro-proxy/server.json

docs.title: Client flags
docs.text:
Flag Env variable Description -server-addr YP_CLIENT_ADDR Server address (host:port) -token YP_CLIENT_TOKEN Bearer token for authentication --format YP_CLIENT_FORMAT Output format: json, table, raw, text --raw -- Compact JSON (overrides --format) -q / --quiet -- Suppress output on success

When stdout is a TTY, the default format is json (pretty-printed). When piped, it switches to raw (compact JSON). The docs tool defaults to text, which prints the document unescaped.

Values are coerced to the type declared in the tool's JSON Schema, including nullable types and nested dot-notation paths (for example params.max_requests_per_second=100 is sent as a number, not a string).

docs.title: Client examples
docs.text:
# Query proxy status (auto-detect server from server.json)
yorishiro-proxy client query resource=status

# Start a listener
yorishiro-proxy client proxy_start listen_addr=127.0.0.1:8080

# List flows with filters
yorishiro-proxy client query resource=flows limit=20 filter.method=POST

# Replay a request
yorishiro-proxy client resend_http flow_id=abc123

# Configure upstream proxy
yorishiro-proxy client configure upstream_proxy=http://proxy:8888

# Positional arguments (tool-specific)
yorishiro-proxy client query flows         # equivalent to resource=flows
yorishiro-proxy client query flow abc123   # equivalent to resource=flow id=abc123

# Explicit connection to a specific server
yorishiro-proxy client -server-addr 127.0.0.1:4000 -token my-token query resource=status

# Pipe output to jq
yorishiro-proxy client query resource=flows --format raw | jq '.[] | select(.method == "POST")'

# Per-tool help (no server connection needed)
yorishiro-proxy client query --help

# Read the docs tool through a running server
yorishiro-proxy client docs topic=fuzz_http section="Macro hook scopes"

docs.title: docs
docs.text:
Print yorishiro-proxy's own documentation without contacting a server. The documents are embedded in the binary, so this works offline — useful when you are still setting up the proxy, or when driving it from CLI-based workflows. It serves the same corpus as the docs MCP tool.

yorishiro-proxy docs [topic] [section] [flags]
Argument / flag Description topic Document to print. Omit to list every topic. Every MCP tool name is a topic (query, macro, fuzz_http, ...), plus getting-started, examples, template-syntax, and docs section Print only this section. Accepts the heading text or its GitHub-style slug, case-insensitively; sub-sections are included --section <heading> Same as the second positional argument

An unknown topic prints the list of valid topics; an unknown section prints that topic's heading outline. Both exit non-zero. Output is plain Markdown with no ANSI styling.

# List every topic with its estimated token size
yorishiro-proxy docs

# Print the whole macro reference
yorishiro-proxy docs macro

# Print a single section (heading text or slug)
yorishiro-proxy docs macro "Variable substitution syntax"
yorishiro-proxy docs macro --section variable-substitution-syntax

docs.title: install
docs.text:
Install and configure yorishiro-proxy components.

yorishiro-proxy install [target] [flags]

docs.title: Targets
docs.text:
Target Description (none) Install all components (MCP + CA) mcp Register MCP configuration only ca Generate CA certificate only playwright Configure Playwright integration (auto-detects browser, installs if needed, applies --no-sandbox in containers)

skills target removed

The previous skills target and --skills-dir flag were removed when vulnerability-verification playbooks migrated to MCP Prompts. Playbooks ship inside the binary and are delivered to the MCP host over prompts/list — no filesystem install needed.

docs.title: Flags
docs.text: Flag Default Description --interactive false Enable interactive prompts (wizard mode) --user-scope false Register in user scope (~/.claude/settings.json) instead of project (.mcp.json) --listen-addr 127.0.0.1:8080 Proxy listen address --trust false Register CA in OS trust store (requires sudo). Only valid with ca target or no target --ca-dir -- CA certificate output directory

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
# Install all components
yorishiro-proxy install

# Register MCP configuration only
yorishiro-proxy install mcp

# Generate CA and register in OS trust store
yorishiro-proxy install ca --trust

# Interactive wizard mode
yorishiro-proxy install --interactive

# Register MCP in user scope
yorishiro-proxy install mcp --user-scope

docs.title: upgrade
docs.text:
Check for and install updates from GitHub Releases.

yorishiro-proxy upgrade [flags]
Flag Default Description --check false Check for updates without downloading

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
# Check and install the latest version
yorishiro-proxy upgrade

# Check for updates without installing
yorishiro-proxy upgrade --check

After upgrading, the bundled MCP prompt playbooks ship inside the new binary — no separate update step is needed. The new prompt set becomes visible to MCP hosts on the next reconnect.

docs.title: version
docs.text:
Print the current version and exit.

yorishiro-proxy version

docs.title: Server flags reference
docs.text:
These flags apply to the server subcommand (or bare invocation without a subcommand).

Flag Env variable Default Description -config YP_CONFIG -- JSON config file path for proxy defaults -db YP_DB ~/.yorishiro-proxy/yorishiro.db SQLite database path or project name -ca-cert YP_CA_CERT -- CA certificate file path -ca-key YP_CA_KEY -- CA private key file path -ca-ephemeral YP_CA_EPHEMERAL false Use ephemeral in-memory CA -insecure YP_INSECURE false Skip upstream TLS certificate verification -tls-fingerprint YP_TLS_FINGERPRINT firefox TLS fingerprint profile: firefox, chrome, safari, edge, random, none. Case-insensitive; unknown values are rejected at startup -log-level YP_LOG_LEVEL info Log level: debug, info, warn, error -log-format YP_LOG_FORMAT text Log format: text, json -log-file YP_LOG_FILE stderr Log output file path -mcp-http-addr YP_MCP_HTTP_ADDR 127.0.0.1:0 Streamable HTTP listen address (also serves the Web UI); use 0 for OS-assigned port -mcp-http-token YP_MCP_HTTP_TOKEN auto-generated HTTP Bearer auth token -no-http-mcp YP_NO_HTTP_MCP false Disable HTTP MCP transport -stdio-mcp YP_STDIO_MCP false Enable stdio MCP transport in addition to HTTP MCP -open-browser YP_OPEN_BROWSER false Open WebUI in browser when HTTP MCP starts -ui-dir YP_UI_DIR -- Directory for WebUI static files, overrides embedded assets -export-dir YP_EXPORT_DIR ~/.yorishiro-proxy/exports Directory that confines manage export_flows / import_flows file paths. Must already exist when set explicitly. See Export directory -target-policy-file YP_TARGET_POLICY_FILE -- Target scope policy JSON file path. Reloadable with SIGHUP -safety-filter YP_SAFETY_FILTER_ENABLED false Enable SafetyFilter engine -max-concurrent-streams YP_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS 0 HTTP/2 SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS advertised to clients. 0 uses the H2 Layer default (500). Range 1..4294967295 (USK-862)

docs.title: Environment variable naming
docs.text:
All flags accept a YP_ prefixed environment variable as a fallback. To derive the variable name from a flag:

  1. Remove the leading -
  2. Replace hyphens with underscores
  3. Uppercase everything
  4. Add the YP_ prefix

For example, -log-level becomes YP_LOG_LEVEL.

docs.title: Signals
docs.text:
On Unix, sending SIGHUP to the server re-reads the target scope policy and replaces the running Policy Layer without a restart:

kill -HUP <pid>
  • The source is -target-policy-file if set, otherwise the target_scope_policy section of -config.
  • The reload is validated exactly like a boot. An invalid file is rejected (logged) and the current policy is kept.
  • Live connections that the new policy denies are closed. See Target scope.
  • The handler is installed only when one of those flags is set (log line target scope policy reload enabled). Without either flag, SIGHUP terminates the process as before.

Closing the terminal

When the reload handler is active, closing the terminal that launched the server sends SIGHUP and triggers a reload instead of stopping the server. Stop it with SIGINT / SIGTERM instead.

docs.title: Export directory (-export-dir)
docs.text:
All server-side file I/O performed by the manage tool's export_flows and import_flows actions is confined to a single directory:

  • Relative output_path / input_path values resolve against the export directory — not against your working directory or the server's.
  • Absolute paths must lie inside the export directory; anything else is rejected.
  • The default ~/.yorishiro-proxy/exports is created on demand. An explicit -export-dir must already exist and be a directory.
  • query with resource: "status" reports the resolved path as export_dir.

Use a dedicated directory: MCP callers can overwrite any file inside it. The server refuses to start when an operator-owned path — the config file, policy file, CA, database, log file, UI directory, plugin scripts, or TLS material — resolves inside the export directory.

yorishiro-proxy server -export-dir /srv/yorishiro/exports

docs.title: MCP transport modes
docs.text:
By default, the server starts HTTP MCP on a random loopback port. The address and authentication token are written to ~/.yorishiro-proxy/server.json for automatic discovery by the client subcommand and other tools.

Mode Flag Default Description HTTP MCP -mcp-http-addr 127.0.0.1:0 (enabled) Streamable HTTP transport + Web UI Stdio MCP -stdio-mcp disabled Stdin/stdout transport for direct MCP client integration No HTTP MCP -no-http-mcp disabled Disable HTTP MCP (useful with -stdio-mcp for stdio-only mode)

To use stdio mode for direct integration with MCP clients like Claude Code:

# Stdio-only (like pre-v0.14.0 behavior)
yorishiro-proxy server -stdio-mcp -no-http-mcp

To use both transports simultaneously:

# HTTP + stdio (both active)
yorishiro-proxy server -stdio-mcp

docs.title: server.json
docs.text:
When HTTP MCP starts, the server writes its connection details to ~/.yorishiro-proxy/server.json:

[
  {
    "addr": "127.0.0.1:54321",
    "token": "auto-generated-token",
    "pid": 12345,
    "started_at": "2026-03-27T10:00:00Z"
  }
]

This file supports multiple concurrent server instances. Each server appends its entry on startup and removes it on shutdown. Stale entries (dead PIDs) are automatically cleaned up.

The client subcommand reads this file for automatic server discovery when no explicit connection flags are given.

docs.title: Database path resolution (-db)
docs.text:
The -db flag supports three resolution modes:

Input Resolution Example Project name (no extension, no path separator) ~/.yorishiro-proxy/<name>.db -db pentest-2026 Absolute path Used as-is -db /data/project.db Relative path with extension CWD-relative -db ./data.db

When omitted, it defaults to ~/.yorishiro-proxy/yorishiro.db.

Project names make it easy to maintain separate databases per engagement:

# Each project gets its own database in ~/.yorishiro-proxy/
yorishiro-proxy server -db client-audit
yorishiro-proxy server -db pentest-2026
yorishiro-proxy server -db webapp-review

Valid project name characters are: alphanumeric (a-z, A-Z, 0-9), hyphen (-), underscore (_), and dot (.). Names must not start with a dot or contain ...

docs.title: CA certificate modes
docs.text: yorishiro-proxy supports three CA modes for TLS interception:

docs.title: Auto-persist (default)
docs.text: When neither -ca-cert/-ca-key nor -ca-ephemeral is specified, the CA is stored in ~/.yorishiro-proxy/ca/. If the files exist, they are loaded; otherwise a new CA is generated and saved automatically.

docs.title: Explicit
docs.text:
Specify both -ca-cert and -ca-key to load a CA from custom file paths. Both flags must be provided together.

yorishiro-proxy server -ca-cert /path/to/ca.crt -ca-key /path/to/ca.key

docs.title: Ephemeral
docs.text:
Use -ca-ephemeral to generate an in-memory CA that is not persisted. A new CA is created on every startup. This cannot be combined with -ca-cert/-ca-key.

yorishiro-proxy server -ca-ephemeral

docs.title: Usage examples
docs.text:
# Default: HTTP MCP on random loopback port with auto-persist CA
yorishiro-proxy server

# Load proxy configuration from a JSON file
yorishiro-proxy server -config proxy.json

# Use a fixed HTTP MCP address
yorishiro-proxy server -mcp-http-addr 127.0.0.1:3000

# Open the Web UI in a browser on startup
yorishiro-proxy server -mcp-http-addr 127.0.0.1:3000 -open-browser

# Use a project-specific database
yorishiro-proxy server -db pentest-2026

# Use an absolute database path
yorishiro-proxy server -db /data/project.db

# Set project name via environment variable
YP_DB=client-audit yorishiro-proxy server

# Skip upstream TLS verification
yorishiro-proxy server -insecure

# Use the Chrome TLS fingerprint instead of the Firefox default
yorishiro-proxy server -tls-fingerprint chrome

# Disable fingerprint spoofing (standard Go crypto/tls)
yorishiro-proxy server -tls-fingerprint none

# Enable JSON-formatted logging to a file
yorishiro-proxy server -log-format json -log-file /var/log/yorishiro.log

# Enable SafetyFilter engine
yorishiro-proxy server -safety-filter

# Load target scope policy from a dedicated file
yorishiro-proxy server -target-policy-file policy.json

# Stdio MCP for direct MCP client integration (no HTTP)
yorishiro-proxy server -stdio-mcp -no-http-mcp

# Combine multiple options
yorishiro-proxy server -db pentest-2026 -mcp-http-addr 127.0.0.1:3000 -insecure -tls-fingerprint chrome

docs.title: Related pages
docs.text:
• Config file -- JSON config file reference
  • TLS -- TLS interception and certificate configuration
  • Upstream proxy -- Proxy chaining configuration
  • Retention -- Flow retention and cleanup settings

docs.title: Config file
docs.text: yorishiro-proxy can load proxy defaults from a JSON config file. The file format is identical to the proxy_start tool's input, so you can reuse the same JSON structure for both file-based configuration and runtime MCP tool calls.

docs.title: Loading a config file
docs.text:
Pass the config file path using the -config flag or YP_CONFIG environment variable:

yorishiro-proxy -config proxy.json

YP_CONFIG=proxy.json yorishiro-proxy

docs.title: File structure overview
docs.text:
The config file is a single JSON object with the following top-level sections:

{
  "listen_addr": "127.0.0.1:8080",
  "upstream_proxy": "",
  "tls_fingerprint": "firefox",
  "tls_passthrough": [],
  "capture_scope": {},
  "intercept_rules": {},
  "intercept_queue": {},
  "auto_transform": [],
  "tcp_forwards": {},
  "max_body_size": 266338304,
  "max_concurrent_streams": 500,
  "client_cert": "",
  "client_key": "",
  "host_tls": {},
  "socks5_auth": "none",
  "socks5_username": "",
  "socks5_password": "",
  "target_scope_policy": {},
  "safety_filter": {},
  "plugins": []
}

All fields are optional. Only include the sections you need.

docs.title: listen_addr
docs.text:
The TCP address the proxy listens on.

Type Default string "127.0.0.1:8080" 
{
  "listen_addr": "127.0.0.1:9090"
}

docs.title: upstream_proxy
docs.text:
Upstream proxy for proxy chaining on the live MITM data path. Supports HTTP and SOCKS5 proxy URLs. The value is either a plain URL string or a structured object that enables per-listener IP rotation.

Type Default string or object "" (direct connection)

String form -- a single static upstream:

{
  "upstream_proxy": "http://proxy.corp.example:3128"
}

Object form -- static URL or rotating template:

Field Type Description url string Literal upstream URL (http:// or socks5://). Mutually exclusive with url_template. rotation is not allowed with url url_template string URL template expanded by the macro engine. §__nonce§ expands to a fresh UUID per resolution (useful for residential-proxy session rotation). Requires rotation rotation.policy string How often the template is re-expanded: per_request (every outbound dial), per_connection (once per inbound client connection), per_target_host (once per upstream host), sticky (once for the listener's lifetime) 
{
  "upstream_proxy": {
    "url_template": "http://user-session-§__nonce§:pass@gw.residential.example:8000",
    "rotation": {"policy": "per_target_host"}
  }
}

The template is probe-expanded at load time, so a malformed template (wrong scheme, missing port, CR/LF) fails at startup rather than at the first dial. See Upstream proxy for details.

docs.title: tls_fingerprint
docs.text:
TLS ClientHello fingerprint profile for upstream HTTPS connections. Uses uTLS to mimic a browser's TLS fingerprint, evading JA3/JA4-based bot detection. The upstream HTTP/2 connection preface (SETTINGS, WINDOW_UPDATE, pseudo-header order) follows the same profile.

Type Default Valid values string "firefox" firefox, chrome, safari, edge, random, none

Empty or omitted resolves to firefox. Use none to opt out of spoofing and use Go's standard crypto/tls. Values are case-insensitive; an unknown value fails config load.

{
  "tls_fingerprint": "chrome"
}

docs.title: tls_passthrough
docs.text:
List of domain patterns that bypass TLS interception (MITM). Connections to matching hosts are forwarded without decryption.

Type Default string[] []

Supported patterns:

  • Exact match: "example.com"
  • Wildcard: "*.example.com" (matches any subdomain)
{
  "tls_passthrough": ["*.google.com", "*.googleapis.com"]
}

docs.title: capture_scope
docs.text:
Controls which requests are recorded to the flow store. This is passed as a raw JSON object to the proxy engine.

{
  "capture_scope": {
    "include": ["*.target.com"],
    "exclude": ["*.static.target.com"]
  }
}

docs.title: intercept_rules
docs.text:
Configures request/response intercept rules. This is passed as a raw JSON object to the intercept engine.

{
  "intercept_rules": {
    "request": true,
    "response": false
  }
}

docs.title: intercept_queue
docs.text:
Hold-queue defaults for intercepted envelopes. Supports a global timeout / behavior pair and a per-protocol override map (USK-855).

Field Type Default Description timeout_ms integer 300000 Global hold-timeout in ms (min 1000) timeout_behavior string "auto_release" Global behavior on timeout (auto_release or auto_drop) protocol_overrides object Per-protocol overrides keyed by canonical envelope.Protocol (http, ws, grpc, grpc-web, sse, raw, tls-handshake). The literal "http2" is rejected -- HTTP/1 and HTTP/2 both envelope as "http"

Built-in per-protocol defaults raise WS / SSE / gRPC / gRPC-Web hold-timeouts to 60000 ms (60 s) so multi-second intercept review windows on long-lived streams do not race the upstream idle timeout; the WS Layer injects synthetic keepalive pings during a hold (USK-854) so the upstream remains alive for the entire window.

{
  "intercept_queue": {
    "timeout_ms": 300000,
    "timeout_behavior": "auto_release",
    "protocol_overrides": {
      "ws":  {"timeout_ms": 120000},
      "sse": {"timeout_ms": 60000, "timeout_behavior": "auto_drop"}
    }
  }
}

docs.title: auto_transform
docs.text:
Configures auto-transform rules for automatic request/response modification. This is passed as a raw JSON array to the transform pipeline.

{
  "auto_transform": [
    {
      "match": {"header": "Authorization"},
      "set_header": {"Authorization": "Bearer new-token"}
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: tcp_forwards
docs.text:
Maps local listen ports to upstream forwarding configurations. Each value can be a string (legacy format) or a ForwardConfig object with protocol detection and TLS options.

Type Default object {}

String format (legacy) -- forwards raw bytes without L7 parsing:

{
  "tcp_forwards": {
    "5432": "db.internal:5432",
    "6379": "redis.internal:6379"
  }
}

ForwardConfig object format -- enables protocol detection and TLS MITM:

{
  "tcp_forwards": {
    "50051": {
      "target": "api.internal:50051",
      "protocol": "grpc"
    },
    "8443": {
      "target": "backend.internal:443",
      "protocol": "auto",
      "tls": true
    },
    "5432": "db.internal:5432"
  }
}

ForwardConfig fields:

Field Type Default Description target string (required) Upstream host:port address protocol string "auto" L7 protocol: auto, raw, http, http2, grpc, websocket, sse (USK-913) tls bool false Enable client-side TLS MITM termination on the forwarded listen port upstream_tls bool false Wrap the upstream-dial connection in TLS (USK-911 / USK-916). Independent of tls upstream_insecure_skip_verify bool inherit -insecure Per-entry override for upstream TLS certificate verification when upstream_tls=true: true to skip verification on this entry, false to enforce, or omit to inherit the global flag (USK-918)

docs.title: TLS × UpstreamTLS matrix
docs.text:
tls controls the listener-side handshake; upstream_tls controls the upstream-side handshake. They are independent and never inferred from target's scheme/port:

tls upstream_tls Client wire Upstream wire Typical use case false false plaintext plaintext Raw L4/L7 forwarding (default) true false TLS plaintext TLS termination only (downstream offload) false true plaintext TLS Plaintext client -> TLS-only upstream true true TLS TLS Full MITM: terminate then re-encrypt upstream

Both formats can be mixed in the same object. Legacy string values are equivalent to {"target": "host:port", "protocol": "raw"}.

docs.title: max_body_size
docs.text:
Per-message body cap shared by HTTP/1.x, HTTP/2, gRPC, gRPC-Web, WebSocket, and SSE. Bodies up to body_spill_threshold (default 10 MiB) stay in memory; the surplus is spilled to a temp file. Exceeding the cap surfaces a per-protocol stream error rather than silently truncating.

Type Default integer (bytes) 266338304 (≈ 254 MiB)

docs.title: max_concurrent_streams
docs.text:
HTTP/2 SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS value advertised to clients. Raised from 100 to 500 in USK-862; range 1..65535. The same knob is exposed at runtime via proxy_start.max_concurrent_streams and configure.max_concurrent_streams.

Type Default integer 500

docs.title: SOCKS5 authentication
docs.text:
Configure SOCKS5 proxy authentication.

Field Type Default Description socks5_auth string "none" Authentication method: none or password socks5_username string "" Username for password authentication socks5_password string "" Password for password authentication 
{
  "socks5_auth": "password",
  "socks5_username": "user",
  "socks5_password": "secret"
}

docs.title: Global client certificate
docs.text:
Configure a global mTLS client certificate for upstream connections. Both client_cert and client_key must be provided together.

Field Type Description client_cert string Path to PEM-encoded client certificate client_key string Path to PEM-encoded client private key 
{
  "client_cert": "/path/to/client.crt",
  "client_key": "/path/to/client.key"
}

docs.title: Per-host TLS (host_tls)
docs.text:
Configure TLS settings for specific hosts. Supports per-host client certificates, custom CA bundles, and TLS verification control. Wildcard patterns (e.g., *.example.com) are supported.

Each entry supports:

Field Type Default Description client_cert string -- PEM-encoded client certificate path client_key string -- PEM-encoded client private key path tls_verify bool\|null null (use global) TLS verification: true = enforce, false = skip, null = global setting ca_bundle string -- PEM-encoded CA bundle file path 
{
  "host_tls": {
    "api.internal.corp": {
      "client_cert": "/path/to/api-client.crt",
      "client_key": "/path/to/api-client.key"
    },
    "*.staging.example.com": {
      "tls_verify": false
    },
    "private-ca.example.com": {
      "ca_bundle": "/path/to/custom-ca.pem",
      "tls_verify": true
    }
  }
}

docs.title: SafetyFilter (safety_filter)
docs.text:
The SafetyFilter engine blocks or masks destructive payloads. This is a Policy Layer setting -- once loaded from a config file, it cannot be modified at runtime via MCP tools.

Field Type Default Description enabled bool false Enable the SafetyFilter engine input object -- Input (request) filter rules output object -- Output (response) filter rules

docs.title: Input filter rules
docs.text:
Input rules inspect outgoing requests and can block destructive payloads.

Field Type Default Description action string "block" Default action: block or log_only rules array [] List of filter rules

docs.title: Output filter rules
docs.text:
Output rules inspect incoming responses and can mask sensitive data.

Field Type Default Description action string "mask" Default action: mask or log_only rules array [] List of filter rules

docs.title: Rule definition
docs.text:
Each rule is either a preset reference or a custom rule. The two are mutually exclusive.

Field Type Description preset string Built-in preset name (e.g., destructive-sql). Mutually exclusive with pattern id string Unique identifier. Required for custom rules name string Human-readable label. Optional pattern string Regular expression pattern. Mutually exclusive with preset targets string[] Parts to inspect. Input: body, url, query, header, headers. Output: body, header:<name>, headers replacement string Override replacement string for output preset rules

docs.title: SafetyFilter example
docs.text:
{
  "safety_filter": {
    "enabled": true,
    "input": {
      "action": "block",
      "rules": [
        {"preset": "destructive-sql"},
        {"preset": "destructive-os-command"},
        {
          "id": "block-drop-api",
          "name": "Block dangerous API calls",
          "pattern": "DELETE\\s+/api/v[0-9]+/(users|accounts)",
          "targets": ["url"]
        }
      ]
    },
    "output": {
      "action": "mask",
      "rules": [
        {"preset": "credit-card"},
        {"preset": "email"},
        {
          "id": "mask-internal-ip",
          "name": "Mask internal IPs",
          "pattern": "10\\.\\d+\\.\\d+\\.\\d+",
          "targets": ["body"]
        }
      ]
    }
  }
}

docs.title: Target scope policy (target_scope_policy)
docs.text:
Target scope policy rules control which network targets the proxy is allowed to access. These rules are part of the Policy Layer: MCP tools cannot change them. Only the operator can replace them at runtime, by editing the source file and sending SIGHUP to the server (see Signals).

Note

When a dedicated policy file is specified via -target-policy-file / YP_TARGET_POLICY_FILE, the target_scope_policy section in the config file is ignored. It is still validated at load.

docs.title: Structure
docs.text: Field Type Description allows array Rules that permit network access. When non-empty, only matching targets are allowed denies array Rules that block network access. Deny rules take precedence over allow rules rate_limits object Rate limiting configuration budget object Diagnostic session budget

docs.title: Target rule fields
docs.text:
All non-empty fields must match for a rule to apply (AND logic).

Field Type Description hostname string Target hostname (case-insensitive). Supports *.example.com wildcard, IPv4 literals, and IPv6 literals bare (::1) or bracketed ([::1]). Empty = any host ports int[] Restrict to specific port numbers (1-65535). Empty = all ports path_prefix string Literal, case-sensitive prefix of the URL path (not a glob). Must start with /. Empty = all paths schemes string[] http (plaintext) or https (TLS), case-insensitive. WebSocket and raw TCP traffic is scoped as http / https too. Empty = all schemes

Rules are validated at load. A rule that could never match — which would silently turn a deny into a no-op — is rejected with an error:

  • hostname with a trailing dot (internal.corp.), a port (host:443), a URL, or a wildcard over an IP literal (*.10.0.0.1)
  • path_prefix without a leading /, or containing *, ?, or # (write /api/, not /api/*)
  • schemes values other than http / https, including ""
  • negative rate_limits or budget values

docs.title: Rate limits (rate_limits)
docs.text:
Rate limiting for AI agent request throttling. These are Policy Layer limits that the Agent Layer cannot exceed.

Field Type Default Description max_requests_per_second float 0 (unlimited) Global rate limit (requests per second) max_requests_per_host_per_second float 0 (unlimited) Per-host rate limit (requests per second)

docs.title: Budget (budget)
docs.text:
Diagnostic session budgets to prevent runaway AI agents.

Field Type Default Description max_total_requests int 0 (unlimited) Maximum number of requests in the session max_duration string "" (unlimited) Maximum session duration (e.g., "30m", "1h")

docs.title: Target scope policy example
docs.text:
{
  "target_scope_policy": {
    "allows": [
      {"hostname": "*.target.com"},
      {"hostname": "api.example.com", "ports": [443], "schemes": ["https"]}
    ],
    "denies": [
      {"hostname": "*.internal.corp"},
      {"hostname": "*.target.com", "path_prefix": "/admin"}
    ],
    "rate_limits": {
      "max_requests_per_second": 50,
      "max_requests_per_host_per_second": 10
    },
    "budget": {
      "max_total_requests": 10000,
      "max_duration": "1h"
    }
  }
}

You can also store target scope policy in a separate file and load it with -target-policy-file. The file format is the same as the target_scope_policy section. Decoding is strict: the file must be a single JSON object, and an unknown key (for example a misspelled "denys") is rejected instead of loading as an empty, allow-all policy.

{
  "allows": [
    {"hostname": "*.target.com"}
  ],
  "denies": [
    {"hostname": "*.internal.corp"}
  ],
  "rate_limits": {
    "max_requests_per_second": 50
  }
}

docs.title: Plugins (plugins)
docs.text:
Configure Starlark-based plugins for the proxy pipeline. Each entry specifies a script path and configuration. Plugins are executed in order.

{
  "plugins": [
    {
      "path": "/path/to/plugin.star",
      "target": "http",
      "hooks": ["on_request", "on_response"],
      "on_error": "log"
    }
  ]
}

For details on writing plugins, see the plugin development guide.

docs.title: Minimal configuration
docs.text:
A minimal config file that sets just the listen address:

{
  "listen_addr": "127.0.0.1:8080"
}

docs.title: Standard assessment configuration
docs.text:
A typical configuration for a vulnerability assessment engagement:

{
  "listen_addr": "127.0.0.1:8080",
  "tls_fingerprint": "chrome",
  "tls_passthrough": ["*.google.com", "*.googleapis.com"],
  "target_scope_policy": {
    "allows": [
      {"hostname": "*.target.com"}
    ],
    "denies": [
      {"hostname": "*.internal.corp"}
    ],
    "rate_limits": {
      "max_requests_per_second": 50,
      "max_requests_per_host_per_second": 10
    },
    "budget": {
      "max_total_requests": 10000,
      "max_duration": "2h"
    }
  },
  "safety_filter": {
    "enabled": true,
    "input": {
      "action": "block",
      "rules": [
        {"preset": "destructive-sql"},
        {"preset": "destructive-os-command"}
      ]
    },
    "output": {
      "action": "mask",
      "rules": [
        {"preset": "credit-card"},
        {"preset": "email"}
      ]
    }
  }
}

docs.title: Full configuration
docs.text:
A comprehensive configuration demonstrating all available sections:

{
  "listen_addr": "127.0.0.1:8080",
  "upstream_proxy": "http://proxy.corp.example:3128",
  "tls_fingerprint": "firefox",
  "tls_passthrough": ["*.google.com"],
  "capture_scope": {
    "include": ["*.target.com"],
    "exclude": ["*.static.target.com"]
  },
  "intercept_rules": {
    "request": true,
    "response": false
  },
  "auto_transform": [
    {
      "match": {"header": "Authorization"},
      "set_header": {"Authorization": "Bearer updated-token"}
    }
  ],
  "tcp_forwards": {
    "5432": "db.internal:5432",
    "50051": {
      "target": "api.internal:50051",
      "protocol": "grpc"
    }
  },
  "client_cert": "/path/to/client.crt",
  "client_key": "/path/to/client.key",
  "host_tls": {
    "api.internal.corp": {
      "client_cert": "/path/to/api-client.crt",
      "client_key": "/path/to/api-client.key"
    },
    "*.staging.example.com": {
      "tls_verify": false
    }
  },
  "socks5_auth": "password",
  "socks5_username": "user",
  "socks5_password": "secret",
  "target_scope_policy": {
    "allows": [
      {"hostname": "*.target.com"}
    ],
    "denies": [
      {"hostname": "*.internal.corp"}
    ],
    "rate_limits": {
      "max_requests_per_second": 50,
      "max_requests_per_host_per_second": 10
    },
    "budget": {
      "max_total_requests": 10000,
      "max_duration": "1h"
    }
  },
  "safety_filter": {
    "enabled": true,
    "input": {
      "action": "block",
      "rules": [
        {"preset": "destructive-sql"},
        {"preset": "destructive-os-command"}
      ]
    },

      "action": "mask",
      "rules": [
        {"preset": "credit-card"},
        {"preset": "email"}
      ]

  },
  "plugins": [
    {
      "path": "/path/to/plugin.star",

      "hooks": ["on_request", "on_response"],
      "on_error": "log"
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Retention
docs.text: yorishiro-proxy can automatically clean up old flows to manage database size. The retention system runs as a background task that periodically removes flows exceeding the configured limits.

docs.title: Settings overview
docs.text:
Setting JSON field Type Default Description Max flows retention_max_flows int 0 (unlimited) Maximum number of flows to retain Max age retention_max_age duration 0 (unlimited) Maximum age of flows to retain Cleanup interval cleanup_interval duration 1h Interval between automatic cleanup runs

All three settings are configured at the application level (not in the proxy config file). They are set via the Config struct fields and take effect at startup.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The flow cleaner is a background goroutine that runs at the configured cleanup_interval. On each run, it:

  1. Removes excess flows -- If retention_max_flows is set and the total flow count exceeds the limit, the oldest flows are deleted first.
  2. Removes expired flows -- If retention_max_age is set, flows older than the specified duration are deleted.

The cleaner only starts if at least one retention policy is configured (retention_max_flows > 0 or retention_max_age > 0). When neither is set, no cleanup runs and all flows are retained indefinitely.

docs.title: Duration format
docs.text:
Duration values use Go's duration string format:

Suffix Meaning Example s Seconds 30s m Minutes 15m h Hours 24h

You can combine units: 1h30m, 2h45m, 72h.

docs.title: Limit by flow count
docs.text:
Keep only the most recent 10,000 flows:

{
  "retention_max_flows": 10000
}

docs.title: Limit by age
docs.text:
Remove flows older than 7 days:

{
  "retention_max_age": "168h"
}

docs.title: Combined limits
docs.text:
Keep at most 5,000 flows and remove anything older than 24 hours, with cleanup running every 30 minutes:

{
  "retention_max_flows": 5000,
  "retention_max_age": "24h",
  "cleanup_interval": "30m"
}

docs.title: Frequent cleanup
docs.text:
For high-traffic environments, reduce the cleanup interval:

{
  "retention_max_flows": 50000,
  "cleanup_interval": "5m"
}

docs.title: Disable automatic cleanup
docs.text:
Set cleanup_interval to 0 to disable the background cleaner. Note that this means flows will accumulate indefinitely even if retention_max_flows or retention_max_age is set:

{
  "cleanup_interval": "0s"
}

docs.title: Validation rules
docs.text:
The following validation rules apply:

  • retention_max_flows must be >= 0. A value of 0 means unlimited (no flow count limit).
  • retention_max_age must be >= 0. A value of 0 means unlimited (no age limit).
  • cleanup_interval must be >= 0. A value of 0 disables automatic cleanup. The default is 1h.

docs.title: TLS
docs.text: yorishiro-proxy provides fine-grained control over TLS behavior for upstream connections. You can spoof TLS fingerprints, bypass MITM for specific domains, configure mTLS client certificates, and manage TLS verification on a per-host basis.

docs.title: TLS fingerprinting
docs.text: When connecting to upstream HTTPS servers, yorishiro-proxy uses uTLS to mimic a real browser's TLS ClientHello. This helps evade JA3/JA4-based bot detection systems.

docs.title: Available profiles
docs.text: Profile Description firefox Mimics Mozilla Firefox's TLS fingerprint (default) chrome Mimics Google Chrome's TLS fingerprint safari Mimics Apple Safari's TLS fingerprint edge Mimics Microsoft Edge's TLS fingerprint random Randomly selects a profile for each connection none Uses Go's standard crypto/tls stack (no fingerprint spoofing)

docs.title: Setting the fingerprint profile
docs.text:
CLI flag:

yorishiro-proxy -tls-fingerprint firefox

Environment variable:

YP_TLS_FINGERPRINT=firefox yorishiro-proxy

Config file:

{
  "tls_fingerprint": "firefox"
}

Runtime change via MCP:

// configure
{
  "tls_fingerprint": "safari"
}

The fingerprint is runtime-mutable: subsequent outbound dials use the new profile, while connections already pinned to a pooled upstream Layer retain the fingerprint they were established with.

When nothing is configured, the profile resolves to firefox on every path — live MITM traffic, resend, and fuzz. Set none to opt out of spoofing entirely. Values are case-insensitive, and an unknown value (for example a typo like firefx) is rejected at config load, at the -tls-fingerprint flag, and by the proxy_start / configure tools, instead of silently falling back to a Go-native ClientHello.

docs.title: HTTP/2 fingerprint
docs.text:
Anti-bot frontends also fingerprint a client's HTTP/2 behavior. With firefox selected, the upstream HTTP/2 connection preface matches Firefox as well:

Element Firefox shape SETTINGS (wire order) HEADER_TABLE_SIZE=65536, ENABLE_PUSH=0, INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE=131072, MAX_FRAME_SIZE=16384 Connection WINDOW_UPDATE 12517377 Request pseudo-header order :method :path :authority :scheme

This corresponds to the Akamai H2 fingerprint 1:65536;2:0;4:131072;5:16384|12517377|0|m,p,a,s. There is no separate setting — the H2 shape follows tls_fingerprint.

Limitations

  • Only firefox has a dedicated H2 profile. chrome, edge, safari, random, and none use the default (Chrome-shaped) H2 behavior.
  • Firefox's PRIORITY frame tree is not reproduced.
  • Both the TLS ClientHello and the H2 shape are pinned to Firefox 120, the newest Firefox profile uTLS ships. An anti-detect browser advertising a newer Firefox user agent shows a small version skew, but the fingerprint is still a genuine Firefox fingerprint.
  • HTTP/3 / QUIC is out of scope: the proxy advertises only h2 and http/1.1 via ALPN.

docs.title: Client fingerprint capture (JA3 / JA4)
docs.text:
On the MITM path, yorishiro-proxy also computes the JA3 and JA4 fingerprints of the client's ClientHello (your browser or tool). They are recorded with the stream and surface as:

  • tls_client_ja3 / tls_client_ja4 in the conn_info of a query flow result
  • ja3 / ja4 keys on ctx.tls and in the tls.on_handshake hook data for plugins

This is capture only: the client's fingerprint is not mirrored to the upstream dial (the upstream uses tls_fingerprint). ClientHellos larger than 4 KiB are not fingerprinted. Passthrough connections are fingerprinted too, and the values appear on the TLS handshake audit flow.

docs.title: TLS passthrough
docs.text: TLS passthrough lets you specify domains that should bypass MITM interception entirely. Connections to matching hosts are forwarded as raw TCP tunnels without decryption. This is useful for certificate-pinned applications or traffic you don't need to inspect.

docs.title: Supported patterns
docs.text:
• Exact match: "example.com" -- matches only example.com
  • Wildcard: "*.example.com" -- matches any subdomain of example.com

docs.title: Config file
docs.text:
{
  "tls_passthrough": [
    "*.google.com",
    "*.googleapis.com",
    "certificate-pinned.example.com"
  ]
}

docs.title: Runtime configuration via MCP
docs.text:
Add patterns incrementally:

// configure
{
  "tls_passthrough": {
    "add": ["*.apple.com", "*.icloud.com"]
  }
}

Remove patterns:

// configure
{
  "tls_passthrough": {
    "remove": ["*.apple.com"]
  }
}

Replace the entire list:

// configure
{
  "operation": "replace",
  "tls_passthrough": {
    "patterns": ["*.google.com", "*.googleapis.com"]
  }
}

docs.title: mTLS client certificates
docs.text: When upstream servers require mutual TLS (mTLS) authentication, you can configure client certificates globally or per host.

docs.title: Global client certificate
docs.text:
Set a default client certificate used for all upstream connections. Both client_cert and client_key must be provided together.

Config file:

{
  "client_cert": "/path/to/client.crt",
  "client_key": "/path/to/client.key"
}

Runtime change via MCP:

// configure
{
  "client_cert": {
    "cert_path": "/path/to/client.crt",
    "key_path": "/path/to/client.key"
  }
}

To remove the global client certificate at runtime:

// configure
{
  "client_cert": {
    "cert_path": "",
    "key_path": ""
  }
}

docs.title: Per-host client certificates
docs.text:
Use the host_tls section to assign different client certificates to specific hosts. Per-host settings override the global client certificate for matching hosts.

{
  "host_tls": {
    "api.internal.corp": {
      "client_cert": "/path/to/api-client.crt",
      "client_key": "/path/to/api-client.key"
    },
    "payments.example.com": {
      "client_cert": "/path/to/payments-client.crt",
      "client_key": "/path/to/payments-client.key"
    }
  }
}

Wildcard patterns are supported:

{
  "host_tls": {
    "*.internal.corp": {
      "client_cert": "/path/to/internal-client.crt",
      "client_key": "/path/to/internal-client.key"
    }
  }
}

docs.title: TLS verification control
docs.text: By default, yorishiro-proxy verifies upstream TLS certificates. You can disable verification globally or per host.

docs.title: Global verification skip
docs.text:
Disable TLS verification for all upstream connections using the -insecure flag. This is useful when targets use self-signed or expired certificates.

yorishiro-proxy -insecure

Or via environment variable:

YP_INSECURE=true yorishiro-proxy

Warning

Disabling TLS verification removes security checks on upstream connections. Only use this when necessary, such as during vulnerability assessments against development environments.

docs.title: Per-host verification
docs.text:
Use host_tls entries to control verification per host. The tls_verify field accepts three states:

Value Behavior true Enforce TLS verification for this host (overrides -insecure) false Skip TLS verification for this host null (omitted) Use the global setting 
{
  "host_tls": {
    "*.staging.example.com": {
      "tls_verify": false
    },
    "production.example.com": {
      "tls_verify": true
    }
  }
}

docs.title: Custom CA bundles
docs.text:
When an upstream server uses a private CA, you can specify a custom CA bundle per host:

{
  "host_tls": {
    "private-ca.example.com": {
      "ca_bundle": "/path/to/custom-ca.pem",
      "tls_verify": true
    }
  }
}

docs.title: host_tls reference
docs.text:
Each entry in the host_tls map is keyed by a hostname or wildcard pattern and supports the following fields:

Field Type Default Description client_cert string -- Path to PEM-encoded client certificate client_key string -- Path to PEM-encoded client private key tls_verify bool\|null null (use global) TLS verification: true = enforce, false = skip, null = global setting ca_bundle string -- Path to PEM-encoded CA bundle file

docs.title: Combined example
docs.text:
A comprehensive host_tls configuration combining mTLS, verification control, and custom CA:

{
  "tls_fingerprint": "firefox",
  "tls_passthrough": ["*.google.com"],
  "client_cert": "/path/to/default-client.crt",
  "client_key": "/path/to/default-client.key",
  "host_tls": {
    "api.internal.corp": {
      "client_cert": "/path/to/api-client.crt",
      "client_key": "/path/to/api-client.key"
    },
    "*.staging.example.com": {
      "tls_verify": false
    },
    "private-ca.example.com": {
      "ca_bundle": "/path/to/custom-ca.pem",
      "tls_verify": true
    },
    "*.dev.example.com": {
      "client_cert": "/path/to/dev-client.crt",
      "client_key": "/path/to/dev-client.key",
      "tls_verify": false
    }
  }
}

docs.title: Upstream proxy
docs.text: yorishiro-proxy can chain through an upstream HTTP or SOCKS5 proxy, routing all outgoing traffic through it. This is useful when you need to access targets behind a corporate proxy, tunnel traffic through a VPN, or combine multiple proxy tools.

docs.title: Supported protocols
docs.text: Protocol URL format Description HTTP proxy http://host:port Standard HTTP CONNECT proxy SOCKS5 proxy socks5://host:port SOCKS5 proxy with optional authentication

docs.title: Config file
docs.text: Set the upstream_proxy field in your config file to route all proxy traffic through an upstream proxy:

docs.title: HTTP proxy
docs.text:
{
  "upstream_proxy": "http://proxy.corp.example:3128"
}

docs.title: HTTP proxy with authentication
docs.text:
{
  "upstream_proxy": "http://user:password@proxy.corp.example:3128"
}

docs.title: SOCKS5 proxy
docs.text:
{
  "upstream_proxy": "socks5://socks-proxy.example:1080"
}

docs.title: SOCKS5 proxy with authentication
docs.text:
{
  "upstream_proxy": "socks5://user:password@socks-proxy.example:1080"
}

docs.title: IP rotation
docs.text:
Instead of a single static URL, you can give a listener a URL template that is re-expanded according to a rotation policy. This is designed for residential or rotating proxy gateways that select the exit IP from a session token in the username.

{
  "upstream_proxy": {
    "url_template": "http://user-session-§__nonce§:password@gw.residential.example:8000",
    "rotation": {"policy": "per_connection"}
  }
}

The template uses the macro §var§ syntax. On the live data path, the only available variable is §__nonce§, which expands to a fresh UUID each time the template is resolved.

rotation.policy A new URL is minted... per_request at every outbound TCP dial per_connection once per inbound client connection per_target_host once per upstream host for the listener sticky once for the listener's lifetime

Rules for the object form:

  • Exactly one of url or url_template must be set.
  • rotation is required with url_template and not allowed with url.
  • The template must expand to an http:// or socks5:// URL with an explicit port. It is probe-expanded when the config is applied, so mistakes fail at startup (or in the tool call), not at the first dial.

The same object is accepted by the proxy_start and configure tools. query with resource: "config" and the configure response report a rotating listener through upstream_proxy_template (credentials redacted) and upstream_proxy_rotation_policy instead of upstream_proxy.

docs.title: Per-iteration rotation in resend and fuzz
docs.text:
resend_http and fuzz_http accept their own upstream_proxy.url_template override, independent of the listener setting. In addition to §__nonce§, these templates can use §__iteration§ (the zero-based variant index). fuzz_http re-expands the template for every variant, so each variant can exit from a distinct IP.

// fuzz_http
{
  "flow_id": "abc123",
  "positions": [
    {"path": "raw_query", "payloads": ["id=1", "id=2", "id=3"]}
  ],
  "upstream_proxy": {
    "url_template": "http://user-session-§__nonce§:password@gw.residential.example:8000"
  }
}

docs.title: Runtime configuration via MCP
docs.text: You can set or change the upstream proxy at runtime using the configure tool. This takes effect immediately for new connections.

docs.title: Enable proxy chaining
docs.text:
// configure
{
  "upstream_proxy": "http://proxy.corp.example:3128"
}

docs.title: Switch to a SOCKS5 proxy
docs.text:
// configure
{
  "upstream_proxy": "socks5://socks-proxy.example:1080"
}

docs.title: Enable rotation on a listener
docs.text:
// configure
{
  "name": "default",
  "upstream_proxy": {
    "url_template": "socks5://user-§__nonce§:pass@gw.residential.example:1080",
    "rotation": {"policy": "per_target_host"}
  }
}

docs.title: Disable proxy chaining
docs.text:
Set the value to an empty string to return to direct connections:

// configure
{
  "upstream_proxy": ""
}

docs.title: proxy_start with upstream proxy
docs.text:
You can also specify the upstream proxy when starting a listener:

// proxy_start
{
  "listen_addr": "127.0.0.1:8080",
  "upstream_proxy": "http://proxy.corp.example:3128"
}

docs.title: Corporate proxy with TLS fingerprinting
docs.text:
Route traffic through a corporate proxy while using browser TLS fingerprinting:

{
  "listen_addr": "127.0.0.1:8080",
  "upstream_proxy": "http://proxy.corp.example:3128",
  "tls_fingerprint": "firefox"
}

docs.title: SOCKS5 tunnel with target scope
docs.text:
Chain through a SOCKS5 proxy and restrict the proxy to specific targets:

{
  "listen_addr": "127.0.0.1:8080",
  "upstream_proxy": "socks5://127.0.0.1:9050",
  "target_scope_policy": {
    "allows": [
      {"hostname": "*.target.com"}
    ]
  }
}

docs.title: Upstream proxy with TLS passthrough
docs.text:
Combine proxy chaining with TLS passthrough to skip MITM for specific domains:

{
  "listen_addr": "127.0.0.1:8080",
  "upstream_proxy": "http://proxy.corp.example:3128",
  "tls_passthrough": ["*.google.com", "*.googleapis.com"]
}

docs.title: Behavior notes
docs.text:
• The upstream proxy setting is per-listener (USK-826). Each proxy_start call carries its own upstream_proxy; one listener can dial direct while another chains through a corporate proxy, and a third rotates through a residential gateway.
  • The upstream proxy setting affects all outgoing connections from the listener, including both HTTP and HTTPS (CONNECT) traffic and dial-time SOCKS5 routing for raw/TCP forwards (USK-797).
  • Changing the upstream proxy at runtime via configure applies to new connections only. Existing connections continue using their original route.
  • Proxy credentials in the URL (e.g., http://user:pass@proxy:3128) are sent as Proxy-Authorization headers for HTTP proxies, or as SOCKS5 username/password authentication (RFC 1929). The SOCKS5 password authenticator is wired into the live data path so credentials work for both control and live dispatch (USK-797).
  • The configure tool's response redacts proxy credentials for security.

docs.title: Auto-transform rules
docs.text: Auto-transform rules automatically modify matching requests and responses as they pass through the proxy. You can add, set, or remove headers and replace body content based on URL patterns, methods, and header conditions.

docs.title: How auto-transform works
docs.text:
When a message passes through the proxy:

  1. Each enabled auto-transform rule is evaluated in priority order (lower values first)
  2. If all conditions match, the rule's action is applied
  3. Multiple rules can apply to the same message

Mutations happen in place on the typed Envelope.Message and the ordered []envelope.KeyValue headers — auto-transform is envelope-native. Subsequent Pipeline Steps see the modified message without envelope replacement.

docs.title: Per-protocol rule engines
docs.text:
The Pipeline TransformStep dispatches via a type-switch on env.Message to a per-protocol transform engine:

Message type Engine HTTPMessage internal/rules/http.TransformEngine WSMessage internal/rules/ws.TransformEngine GRPCStartMessage, GRPCDataMessage, GRPCEndMessage internal/rules/grpc.TransformEngine SSEMessage pass-through (half-duplex receive-only)

The configuration shapes documented below target the HTTP engine. WebSocket and gRPC rules use the same priority/condition/action vocabulary adapted to each protocol's message shape (WS frames, gRPC service/method, gRPC trailers).

docs.title: Where auto-transform runs
docs.text: TransformStep sits after Intercept in the canonical Pipeline chain (HostScope → HTTPScope → Budget → Safety → PluginPre → Intercept → Transform → PluginPost → Record), so transforms apply to the live envelope after any operator hold/release decision. Resend and Macro fan-out paths bypass PluginPre and Intercept but still traverse Transform → PluginPost → Record, so synthesized requests pick up the same transforms as proxied traffic.

docs.title: Rule definition
docs.text:
Each auto-transform rule has the following fields:

Field Type Description id string Unique rule identifier enabled boolean Whether the rule is active priority integer Execution order (lower values applied first) direction string "request", "response", or "both" conditions object Matching criteria action object Transformation to apply

docs.title: Matching conditions
docs.text:
Field Type Description url_pattern string Regex matched against the full request URL methods array HTTP method whitelist (case-insensitive) header_match object Header name to regex mapping (AND logic)

All specified conditions must match (AND logic). An empty conditions object matches everything.

docs.title: Set a header
docs.text:
Replace a header value (or add it if not present):

// configure
{
  "auto_transform": {
    "add": [
      {
        "id": "inject-auth",
        "enabled": true,
        "priority": 10,
        "direction": "request",
        "conditions": {
          "url_pattern": "/api/.*"
        },
        "action": {
          "type": "set_header",
          "header": "Authorization",
          "value": "Bearer test-token-123"
        }
      }
    ]
  }
}

docs.title: Add a header
docs.text:
Add a header value (appends to existing values):

// configure
{
  "auto_transform": {
    "add": [
      {
        "id": "add-proxy-header",
        "enabled": true,
        "priority": 20,
        "direction": "request",
        "conditions": {},
        "action": {
          "type": "add_header",
          "header": "X-Proxied-By",
          "value": "yorishiro-proxy"
        }
      }
    ]
  }
}

docs.title: Remove a header
docs.text:
Remove a header from requests or responses:

// configure
{
  "auto_transform": {
    "add": [
      {
        "id": "strip-csp",
        "enabled": true,
        "priority": 10,
        "direction": "response",
        "conditions": {},
        "action": {
          "type": "remove_header",
          "header": "Content-Security-Policy"
        }
      }
    ]
  }
}

docs.title: Replace body content
docs.text:
Search and replace text in the body using regex:

// configure
{
  "auto_transform": {
    "add": [
      {
        "id": "replace-host",
        "enabled": true,
        "priority": 10,
        "direction": "request",
        "conditions": {},
        "action": {
          "type": "replace_body",
          "pattern": "production\\.example\\.com",
          "value": "staging.example.com"
        }
      }
    ]
  }
}

docs.title: Priority
docs.text:
Rules are applied in priority order, with lower values executed first. This lets you control the order of transformations:

// configure
{
  "auto_transform": {
    "add": [
      {
        "id": "step-1",
        "enabled": true,
        "priority": 10,
        "direction": "request",
        "conditions": {},
        "action": {"type": "set_header", "header": "X-Step", "value": "1"}
      },
      {
        "id": "step-2",
        "enabled": true,
        "priority": 20,
        "direction": "request",
        "conditions": {},
        "action": {"type": "set_header", "header": "X-Step", "value": "2"}
      }
    ]
  }
}

In this example, step-1 runs first but step-2 overwrites the header value because it runs second.

docs.title: Enable and disable
docs.text:
// configure
{
  "auto_transform": {
    "disable": ["inject-auth"],
    "enable": ["strip-csp"]
  }
}

docs.title: Remove rules
docs.text:
// configure
{
  "auto_transform": {
    "remove": ["inject-auth"]
  }
}

docs.title: Replace all rules
docs.text:
// configure
{
  "operation": "replace",
  "auto_transform": {
    "rules": [
      {
        "id": "only-rule",
        "enabled": true,
        "priority": 0,
        "direction": "both",
        "conditions": {},
        "action": {
          "type": "add_header",
          "header": "X-Proxy",
          "value": "yorishiro"
        }
      }
    ]
  }
}

docs.title: Inject authentication headers
docs.text:
Automatically add authentication headers to all API requests:

// configure
{
  "auto_transform": {
    "add": [
      {
        "id": "auto-auth",
        "enabled": true,
        "priority": 10,
        "direction": "request",
        "conditions": {
          "url_pattern": "api\\.target\\.com/.*"
        },
        "action": {
          "type": "set_header",
          "header": "Authorization",
          "value": "Bearer your-api-token"
        }
      }
    ]
  }
}

docs.title: Strip security headers for testing
docs.text:
Remove security headers from responses to test client-side behavior:

// configure
{
  "auto_transform": {
    "add": [
      {
        "id": "strip-hsts",
        "enabled": true,
        "priority": 10,
        "direction": "response",
        "conditions": {},
        "action": {"type": "remove_header", "header": "Strict-Transport-Security"}
      },
      {
        "id": "strip-csp",
        "enabled": true,
        "priority": 11,
        "direction": "response",
        "conditions": {},
        "action": {"type": "remove_header", "header": "Content-Security-Policy"}
      },
      {
        "id": "strip-xfo",
        "enabled": true,
        "priority": 12,
        "direction": "response",
        "conditions": {},
        "action": {"type": "remove_header", "header": "X-Frame-Options"}
      }
    ]
  }
}

docs.title: Replace API endpoints
docs.text:
Redirect requests from production to staging:

// configure
{
  "auto_transform": {
    "add": [
      {
        "id": "redirect-to-staging",
        "enabled": true,
        "priority": 10,
        "direction": "request",
        "conditions": {
          "methods": ["POST", "PUT", "DELETE"]
        },
        "action": {
          "type": "replace_body",
          "pattern": "api\\.production\\.com",
          "value": "api.staging.com"
        }
      }
    ]
  }
}

docs.title: Flow export and import
docs.text: You can export recorded flows to share with other tools or team members, and import flows from previous sessions. yorishiro-proxy supports three export formats: JSONL, HAR 1.2, and cURL commands.

docs.title: Export directory
docs.text:
File paths in export_flows (output_path) and import_flows (input_path) are confined to the server's export directory — by default ~/.yorishiro-proxy/exports, configurable with the -export-dir server flag or YP_EXPORT_DIR.

  • Relative paths resolve against the export directory, not against your working directory or the server's.
  • Absolute paths are accepted only if they lie inside the export directory. Anything else — ../ escapes, symlinks pointing outside, absolute paths elsewhere — is rejected.
  • The response's output_path (and the import result's source) is the absolute path of the file.
  • query with resource: "status" reports the directory as export_dir.

This prevents an MCP caller from overwriting operator-owned files such as the policy file, config file, CA key pair, or flow database through an export.

docs.title: JSONL format
docs.text:
JSONL (JSON Lines) is the native export format. Each line is a complete JSON object containing a flow and its messages. This format supports all protocols and flow types, including raw TCP and gRPC.

// manage
{
  "action": "export_flows",
  "params": {
    "format": "jsonl",
    "output_path": "flows.jsonl"
  }
}

When output_path is omitted, small exports (up to 100 flows) are returned inline in the response:

// manage
{
  "action": "export_flows",
  "params": {
    "format": "jsonl"
  }
}

docs.title: HAR 1.2 format
docs.text:
HAR (HTTP Archive) 1.2 is a standard format compatible with browser DevTools, Burp Suite, and OWASP ZAP. HAR export always requires a file path:

// manage
{
  "action": "export_flows",
  "params": {
    "format": "har",
    "output_path": "flows.har"
  }
}

HAR limitations

HAR is an HTTP-specific format. Raw TCP and gRPC flows are excluded from HAR exports. WebSocket flows include a _webSocketMessages custom field. Binary bodies are Base64-encoded with content.encoding: "base64".

docs.title: cURL command format
docs.text:
Export individual flows as cURL commands using the query tool:

// query
{
  "action": "curl",
  "params": {
    "flow_id": "abc-123"
  }
}

docs.title: Filtering exports
docs.text:
Apply filters to export a subset of flows:

// manage
{
  "action": "export_flows",
  "params": {
    "format": "jsonl",
    "filter": {
      "protocol": "HTTPS",
      "url_pattern": "/api/",
      "time_after": "2026-02-01T00:00:00Z",
      "time_before": "2026-02-28T23:59:59Z"
    },
    "output_path": "api-flows.jsonl"
  }
}

docs.title: Filter fields
docs.text: Field Type Description protocol string Filter by protocol (e.g. "HTTPS", "HTTP/1.x", "WebSocket") url_pattern string Filter by URL substring time_after string Include flows after this time (RFC3339 format) time_before string Include flows before this time (RFC3339 format)

docs.title: Metadata-only export
docs.text:
Export flow metadata without message bodies for a lightweight overview:

// manage
{
  "action": "export_flows",
  "params": {
    "format": "jsonl",
    "include_bodies": false,
    "output_path": "flows-meta.jsonl"
  }
}

docs.title: Importing flows
docs.text:
Import flows from a JSONL file. Each line must be a valid export record with version "1":

// manage
{
  "action": "import_flows",
  "params": {
    "input_path": "flows.jsonl"
  }
}

docs.title: Conflict handling
docs.text:
When importing flows with IDs that already exist in the store, use on_conflict to control behavior:

Policy Description skip Skip flows with existing IDs (default) replace Delete existing flows and re-import 
// manage
{
  "action": "import_flows",
  "params": {
    "input_path": "flows.jsonl",
    "on_conflict": "replace"
  }
}

docs.title: Import result
docs.text:
The import action returns:

Field Description imported Number of flows successfully imported skipped Number of flows skipped due to conflicts errors Number of flows that failed to import source Absolute path of the import file error_details Details of any import errors

docs.title: Export for external analysis
docs.text:
Export HTTPS flows to HAR for analysis in Burp Suite:

// manage
{
  "action": "export_flows",
  "params": {
    "format": "har",
    "filter": {"protocol": "HTTPS"},
    "output_path": "analysis.har"
  }
}

docs.title: Session backup
docs.text:
Export all flows from a testing session:

// manage
{
  "action": "export_flows",
  "params": {
    "format": "jsonl",
    "output_path": "session-backup.jsonl"
  }
}

docs.title: Restore a session
docs.text:
Import a previous session's flows:

// manage
{
  "action": "import_flows",
  "params": {
    "input_path": "session-backup.jsonl",
    "on_conflict": "skip"
  }
}

docs.title: Time-scoped export
docs.text:
Export flows from a specific time window:

// manage
{
  "action": "export_flows",
  "params": {
    "format": "jsonl",
    "filter": {
      "time_after": "2026-03-14T09:00:00Z",
      "time_before": "2026-03-14T17:00:00Z"
    },
    "output_path": "today.jsonl"
  }
}

docs.title: Fuzzer
docs.text:
The fuzzer executes automated testing campaigns by injecting payloads into recorded proxy requests. You define injection positions and payload lists, then the fuzz tool runs synchronously, records each variant as a new stream, and returns the per-variant result list.

Each protocol has its own typed fuzz tool: fuzz_http, fuzz_ws, fuzz_grpc, fuzz_raw. Pick the tool that matches the recorded flow's protocol.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Select a recorded flow as the template
  2. Define typed positions where payloads should be injected
  3. Call the typed fuzz tool -- it runs synchronously and returns the per-variant result list
  4. Inspect individual variant streams via the query tool keyed by stream_id

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Maximum variants per call: 1000 (cartesian product across all positions)
  • Maximum positions per call: 32
  • Maximum decoded payload size per position: 1 MiB

The variant sequence is the cartesian product of all positions' payloads. Each variant is executed sequentially with a fresh dial.

docs.title: Per-variant gates
docs.text:
Right before each variant is sent, its post-substitution message is checked against the current target scope and then the SafetyFilter. Because the check runs per variant:

  • Positions that rewrite scope-relevant fields (fuzz_http authority / scheme / path / raw_query, fuzz_grpc service / method) are judged on their mutated value, not only on the base request
  • A scope change made mid-run -- an agent security call or a SIGHUP policy reload -- applies from the next variant on

A blocked variant is recorded with an error and no flow, and the run continues.

docs.title: HTTP/2 flows
docs.text: fuzz_http sends every variant over the recorded flow's protocol: a flow captured over HTTP/2 is fuzzed over HTTP/2. Override it with http_version (http/1.1, h2, h2c). See fuzz_http.

docs.title: Position definitions
docs.text:
Positions specify where payloads are injected. Each position has:

  • path -- typed path into the protocol's Message shape
  • payloads -- list of values to substitute at this path
  • encoding -- "text" (default) or "base64"

The position path values for fuzz_http are: method, scheme, authority, path, raw_query, body, headers[N].name, headers[N].value. Cookies live inside the Cookie header; fuzz them via headers[N].value. The legacy body_regex and partial-match match modes are gone -- when you need surgical body edits, combine body_patches (inherited from resend_http) with full-value position payloads.

docs.title: Header position
docs.text:
Replace a header value (find the header's index from the recorded flow):

// fuzz_http
{
  "flow_id": "abc-123",
  "positions": [
    {
      "path": "headers[3].value",
      "payloads": ["Bearer token1", "Bearer token2", "Bearer admin-token"]
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Query position
docs.text:
Inject into a query string -- the typed surface fuzzes the full raw_query:

// fuzz_http
{
  "flow_id": "abc-123",
  "positions": [
    {
      "path": "raw_query",
      "payloads": ["search=foo", "search=<script>alert(1)</script>"]
    }
  ]
}

For more precise per-parameter substitution, pre-compute the candidate query strings and supply them as the payload list.

docs.title: Body position
docs.text:
Substitute the entire request body:

// fuzz_http
{
  "flow_id": "abc-123",
  "positions": [
    {
      "path": "body",
      "payloads": [
        "{\"password\":\"pass1\"}",
        "{\"password\":\"pass2\"}"
      ]
    }
  ]
}

For partial JSON edits, combine body_patches (inherited from resend_http) with one or more body positions.

docs.title: Cookie
docs.text:
Cookies are sent via the Cookie request header. Locate the header's index in the recorded flow and fuzz headers[N].value:

// fuzz_http
{
  "flow_id": "abc-123",
  "positions": [
    {
      "path": "headers[2].value",
      "payloads": ["session=abc", "session=def", "session=admin"]
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Payload encoding
docs.text:
Each position has a single encoding ("text" default or "base64"). Codec chains (the legacy ["base64", "url_encode_query", ...] arrays) are no longer applied at the fuzz tool layer -- pre-encode payloads from the client side or use body_patches with the encoding array for body edits. To inject pre-encoded binary payloads:

// fuzz_http
{
  "flow_id": "abc-123",
  "positions": [
    {
      "path": "body",
      "encoding": "base64",
      "payloads": [
        "PHNjcmlwdD5hbGVydCgxKTwvc2NyaXB0Pg==",
        "JyBPUiAxPTEgLS0="
      ]
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Attack patterns
docs.text: The typed fuzz tools always cartesian-product positions × payloads, capped at 1000 variants. The legacy sequential / parallel distinction no longer exists -- if you need a single-position-at-a-time scan, issue one fuzz call per position. If you need lockstep "zip" semantics, pre-compute the lockstepped payload list and supply it as a single position.

docs.title: Cartesian product example
docs.text:
Two positions × two payloads each = four variants:

// fuzz_http
{
  "flow_id": "abc-123",
  "positions": [
    {"path": "raw_query", "payloads": ["user=admin", "user=root"]},
    {"path": "body", "payloads": ["{\"password\":\"pass1\"}", "{\"password\":\"pass2\"}"]}
  ]
}

docs.title: Execution parameters
docs.text:
The typed tools are synchronous and serial. The legacy concurrency, rate_limit_rps, delay_ms, max_retries parameters have been removed -- pace from the client side by chunking your payload list across multiple calls. Per-variant timeouts use the inherited timeout_ms (default 30000).

Parameter Type Default Description timeout_ms integer 30000 Per-variant timeout in ms tag string Tag stored on every variant Stream's Tags map

docs.title: Synchronous execution
docs.text: The typed fuzz tools run in-process and return the full per-variant result list when finished. There is no separate fuzz-job lifecycle to start, pause, resume, or cancel -- to interrupt a long run, cancel the MCP call from the client. Each variant is recorded as its own stream and remains queryable after the run.

docs.title: Running a campaign
docs.text:
// fuzz_http
{
  "flow_id": "abc-123",
  "positions": [
    {
      "path": "raw_query",
      "payloads": ["q=<script>", "q={{7*7}}", "q=' OR 1=1"]
    }
  ],
  "tag": "xss-scan"
}

The response contains variants[], each with a stream_id, status_code, body_size, the payload map, and per-variant duration_ms. Cancel the MCP call from the client to stop the run mid-campaign.

docs.title: Stop conditions
docs.text:
Each typed tool exposes a single boolean stop flag, picked to match the protocol:

Tool Flag Triggers when fuzz_http stop_on_5xx A variant returns a 5xx response fuzz_ws stop_on_close A variant receives a Close frame from upstream fuzz_grpc stop_on_non_ok A variant returns a non-OK gRPC status fuzz_raw stop_on_error A variant fails (network error, timeout, pipeline drop)

The legacy error_count, latency_threshold_ms, latency_baseline_multiplier, and latency_window conditions are gone -- inspect the returned variants[] rows after the call to apply your own thresholds.

// fuzz_http
{
  "flow_id": "abc-123",
  "positions": [
    {
      "path": "raw_query",
      "payloads": ["id=1", "id=2", "id=3"]
    }
  ],
  "stop_on_5xx": true
}

docs.title: Querying results
docs.text:
Each variant's full request and response are stored under its stream_id. Use the query tool to retrieve them:

// query
{
  "resource": "stream",
  "id": "<variant-stream-id>"
}

The fuzz response itself includes per-variant status_code, body_size, duration_ms, payload map, and any error -- enough to triage results without an extra round trip.

docs.title: Macro hooks
docs.text:
Every typed fuzz tool accepts pre_macro and post_macro hooks that run a stored macro around the variants. Use them to log in, refresh a session, tear down state, or react to specific responses without leaving the fuzz call.

// fuzz_http
{
  "flow_id": "abc-123",
  "headers": [
    {"name": "Authorization", "value": "Bearer §session_token§"}
  ],
  "positions": [
    {"path": "raw_query", "payloads": ["id=1", "id=2", "id=3"]}
  ],
  "pre_macro": {"name": "login-once", "scope": "job"},
  "post_macro": {"name": "alert-on-auth", "run_interval": "on_status", "status_codes": [401, 403]}
}

Key concepts:

  • scope -- "iteration" (default) runs the hook around every variant with a fresh KV Store per variant. "job" runs it once before (pre) or after (post) the whole loop with a KV Store shared by every variant. pre_macro and post_macro can use different scopes.
  • run_interval -- per-variant cadence (scope="iteration" only). pre_macro: always, once, every_n (with n), on_error. post_macro: always, on_status (with status_codes), on_match (with match_pattern).
  • on_error -- what a failing hook does: skip (default) skips the variant (or the whole job for a job-scope pre_macro), abort stops the run, continue proceeds anyway.
  • vars -- static KV Store overrides for the hook. Keys starting with __ are reserved and silently dropped.
  • Reserved response keys -- an iteration-scope post_macro sees the variant's response as __response_* keys. The key set is protocol-specific (for example, fuzz_grpc uses gRPC status codes 0-16, and fuzz_raw has no status at all).

Supplying headers replaces the inherited header list, so include every header the request needs (the example above is abbreviated). fuzz_http expands §var§ templates in the base request and position payloads, and fuzz_ws expands them in position payloads, so values a pre_macro extracts flow straight into the variants. fuzz_grpc and fuzz_raw do not expand templates in the request.

See fuzz_http for the full field reference and the per-protocol differences on fuzz_ws, fuzz_grpc, and fuzz_raw.

docs.title: Upstream proxy rotation
docs.text:
fuzz_http can send each variant through a different upstream proxy -- typically a residential proxy pool that assigns a new exit IP per session ID. The upstream_proxy.url_template is re-expanded per variant with §__iteration§ (variant index) and §__nonce§ (fresh UUID):

// fuzz_http
{
  "flow_id": "abc-123",
  "positions": [
    {"path": "body", "payloads": ["{\"pin\":\"0000\"}", "{\"pin\":\"0001\"}"]}
  ],
  "upstream_proxy": {
    "url_template": "http://user-session-§__nonce§:password@residential.example:8080"
  }
}

See fuzz_http and Upstream proxy.

docs.title: XSS scanning
docs.text:
// fuzz_http
{
  "flow_id": "search-flow",
  "positions": [
    {
      "path": "raw_query",
      "payloads": [
        "q=%3Cscript%3Ealert(1)%3C%2Fscript%3E",
        "q=%3Cimg+src%3Dx+onerror%3Dalert(1)%3E",
        "q=%7B%7B7*7%7D%7D",
        "q=%24%7B7*7%7D"
      ]
    }
  ],
  "tag": "xss-scan"
}

docs.title: Brute force PIN
docs.text:
For exhaustive enumerations like 4-digit PINs, generate the candidate list client-side and chunk across multiple fuzz calls (the per-call cap is 1000 variants):

// fuzz_http
{
  "flow_id": "pin-verify-flow",
  "positions": [
    {
      "path": "body",
      "payloads": [
        "{\"pin\":\"0000\"}",
        "{\"pin\":\"0001\"}",
        "{\"pin\":\"0002\"}"
      ]
    }
  ],
  "stop_on_5xx": false,
  "tag": "pin-brute"
}

docs.title: IDOR enumeration
docs.text:
// fuzz_http
{
  "flow_id": "user-profile-flow",
  "positions": [
    {
      "path": "raw_query",
      "payloads": ["user_id=1", "user_id=2", "user_id=3", "user_id=4"]
    }
  ],
  "tag": "idor-scan"
}
