docs.title: Intercept
docs.text: The intercept feature lets you pause HTTP, WebSocket, and gRPC messages in transit, inspect them, and decide whether to release, modify, or drop them. This gives you real-time control over traffic flowing through the proxy.

docs.title: How interception works
docs.text:
1. Define intercept rules that match specific requests or responses
  2. When a matching message passes through the proxy, it is held in the intercept queue
  3. The AI agent (or WebUI user) reviews the queued item
  4. The item is released as-is, modified and forwarded, or dropped

docs.title: Per-protocol rule engines
docs.text:
The Pipeline InterceptStep dispatches via a type-switch on env.Message to a per-protocol intercept engine:

Message type Engine HTTPMessage internal/rules/http.InterceptEngine WSMessage internal/rules/ws.InterceptEngine GRPCStartMessage, GRPCDataMessage, GRPCEndMessage internal/rules/grpc.InterceptEngine SSEMessage pass-through (half-duplex receive-only, no Send-side rules to apply)

Each engine evaluates protocol-specific match conditions (HTTP path/method, WS opcode, gRPC service/method) and produces the matched rule list.

docs.title: Hold queue
docs.text:
A matched envelope is parked in the HoldQueue (internal/rules/common.HoldQueue) — a thread-safe map of held envelopes keyed by intercept ID. The queue is shared across all protocols. Each held entry waits for an external action (release, drop, or modify-and-forward) delivered via the intercept MCP tool or the Web UI.

The queue is bounded (default 100 items) and time-bounded (default 5 minutes). When either limit is hit, the configured timeout behavior runs (auto_release or auto_drop).

docs.title: Release-time re-checks
docs.text:
Every release — manual release, timeout auto-release, and modify_and_forward — first re-runs the target scope check against the envelope about to be forwarded (the modified one for modify_and_forward), using the rules in force at release time. A deny added while the item was held (a SIGHUP policy reload or a security change), or a rewrite of the authority / path to a denied target, blocks the release: an HTTP request gets 403 with blocked_by: target_scope, a WebSocket / gRPC message is dropped, and the block is recorded as a flow. The intercept call itself still succeeds.

When you choose modify-and-forward, the user-modified envelope is then re-evaluated by SafetyStep before being released downstream. This closes the gap where an operator-injected payload could bypass the input filter that gated the original held envelope (USK-702).

If a policy change revokes the connection while an item is held, the connection is closed only after the hold resolves and its result is recorded.

docs.title: Cancelled holds
docs.text: If a hold ends without an intercept action because the connection or proxy went away (proxy_stop, session teardown, or the peer direction failing), the held request is recorded as an audit stream with state error and blocked_by: intercept_cancelled. Its stream ID equals the held entry's stream_id, so you can find it with query instead of it silently disappearing.

docs.title: Configuring intercept rules
docs.text:
Intercept rules define which requests and responses are captured. You configure rules using the configure tool:

// configure
{
  "intercept_rules": {
    "add": [
      {
        "id": "api-requests",
        "enabled": true,
        "direction": "request",
        "conditions": {
          "host_pattern": "api\\.target\\.com",
          "path_pattern": "/api/.*",
          "methods": ["POST", "PUT", "DELETE"]
        }
      }
    ]
  }
}

docs.title: Rule fields
docs.text: Field Type Description id string Unique rule identifier enabled boolean Whether the rule is active direction string "request", "response", or "both" conditions object Matching criteria

docs.title: Condition fields
docs.text:
Field Type Description host_pattern string Regex matched against the hostname (port excluded) path_pattern string Regex matched against the URL path methods array HTTP method whitelist (case-insensitive) header_match object Header name to regex mapping (AND logic)

All specified conditions must match for a rule to trigger (AND logic).

docs.title: Direction
docs.text:
• request -- intercepts the request before it reaches the upstream server
  • response -- intercepts the response before it reaches the client
  • both -- intercepts both the request and the response

Intercepted items include a phase field ("request" or "response") so you know which direction was captured.

docs.title: Viewing queued items
docs.text:
Use the query tool to list items waiting in the intercept queue:

// query
{
  "action": "intercept_queue"
}

Each queued item has an intercept_id that you use for subsequent actions.

docs.title: Release
docs.text:
Forward the intercepted item as-is, without modifications:

// intercept
{
  "action": "release",
  "params": {
    "intercept_id": "int-abc-123"
  }
}

docs.title: Modify and forward
docs.text:
Modify the intercepted item before forwarding. The available mutation parameters depend on the phase.

Request phase mutations:

// intercept
{
  "action": "modify_and_forward",
  "params": {
    "intercept_id": "int-abc-123",
    "override_method": "POST",
    "override_url": "https://api.target.com/v2/users",
    "override_headers": {"Authorization": "Bearer injected-token"},
    "add_headers": {"X-Custom": "value"},
    "remove_headers": ["X-Debug"],
    "override_body": "{\"role\":\"admin\"}"
  }
}

Response phase mutations:

// intercept
{
  "action": "modify_and_forward",
  "params": {
    "intercept_id": "int-resp-456",
    "override_status": 200,
    "override_response_headers": {"Content-Type": "application/json"},
    "add_response_headers": {"X-Modified": "true"},
    "remove_response_headers": ["X-Server-Info"],
    "override_response_body": "{\"success\": true}"
  }
}

docs.title: Drop
docs.text:
Discard the intercepted item. For HTTP requests, this returns a 403 Forbidden response (blocked_by: intercept_drop) to the client; a WebSocket frame is discarded. Dropping a native gRPC request item (start or a client message) ends the RPC with grpc-status: 7 (PERMISSION_DENIED) and grpc-message: blocked by intercept_drop:

// intercept
{
  "action": "drop",
  "params": {
    "intercept_id": "int-abc-123"
  }
}

docs.title: Request phase parameters
docs.text: Parameter Type Description override_method string Override the HTTP method override_url string Override the target URL override_headers object Header overrides (key-value pairs) add_headers object Headers to add remove_headers array Header names to remove override_body string Override the request body

docs.title: Response phase parameters
docs.text: Parameter Type Description override_status integer Override the HTTP status code override_response_headers object Response header overrides add_response_headers object Response headers to add remove_response_headers array Response header names to remove override_response_body string Override the response body

docs.title: Queue configuration
docs.text:
Configure the intercept queue behavior using the configure tool:

// configure
{
  "intercept_queue": {
    "timeout_ms": 300000,
    "timeout_behavior": "auto_release",
    "protocol_overrides": {
      "ws":  {"timeout_ms": 60000},
      "sse": {"timeout_ms": 60000}
    }
  }
}
Parameter Type Default Description timeout_ms integer 300000 (5 min) Global timeout for held envelopes (minimum 1000 ms) timeout_behavior string auto_release What happens on timeout: auto_release or auto_drop protocol_overrides object Per-protocol timeout/behavior overrides keyed by canonical envelope.Protocol (http, ws, grpc, grpc-web, sse, raw, tls-handshake). null removes a key under merge; replace mode atomically swaps the map

When a blocked request times out:

  • auto_release -- the request is forwarded as-is (default)
  • auto_drop -- the request is dropped with a 502 response

docs.title: Per-protocol hold-timeout defaults
docs.text:
Protocol Default hold-timeout http 300 000 ms ws, sse, grpc, grpc-web 60 000 ms (USK-855) raw, tls-handshake inherit global (300 000 ms)

WebSocket and SSE were raised to 60s so multi-second human reviews on long-lived streams do not race against the upstream's idle timeout. While a WebSocket frame is held, the proxy injects synthetic keepalive pings to the upstream (USK-854) so the connection stays alive for the full hold window. The literal "http2" is not a valid override key -- both HTTP/1 and HTTP/2 envelope as "http".

docs.title: Enable and disable rules
docs.text:
// configure
{
  "intercept_rules": {
    "disable": ["api-requests"],
    "enable": ["other-rule"]
  }
}

docs.title: Remove rules
docs.text:
// configure
{
  "intercept_rules": {
    "remove": ["api-requests"]
  }
}

docs.title: Replace all rules
docs.text:
// configure
{
  "operation": "replace",
  "intercept_rules": {
    "rules": [
      {
        "id": "new-rule",
        "enabled": true,
        "direction": "both",
        "conditions": {
          "path_pattern": "/api/.*"
        }
      }
    ]
  }
}

docs.title: Raw bytes mode
docs.text:
By default, the intercept tool operates in structured mode -- it parses and serializes requests at the HTTP (L7) layer. This means modifications go through the standard HTTP library, which may normalize headers, adjust Content-Length, and apply transfer encoding.

Raw bytes mode bypasses this entirely. When you set "mode": "raw", the proxy sends bytes directly on the wire without any HTTP library processing. This gives you full control over every byte of the request or response.

docs.title: Structured vs raw mode
docs.text: Aspect Structured mode (default) Raw mode Layer L7 (HTTP semantics) L4 (raw bytes on the wire) Modifications override_method, override_headers, etc. raw_override_base64 (entire payload) Normalization HTTP library may adjust headers, Content-Length, encoding None -- bytes are forwarded as-is Auto-transform Applied (e.g., gzip decompression for display) Not applied Use case Standard request/response editing Protocol-level anomaly testing

docs.title: HTTP/1.x raw forwarding
docs.text:
In raw mode for HTTP/1.x, the proxy writes your raw bytes directly to a TCP (or TLS) connection to the upstream server, completely bypassing net/http.Transport. The raw response from upstream is read back and forwarded to the client as-is.

This enables testing scenarios where HTTP library normalization would otherwise mask the issue:

  • HTTP Request Smuggling -- craft requests with conflicting Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding headers (CL/TE, TE/CL)
  • Header injection -- send malformed headers that a standard HTTP library would reject or rewrite
  • Protocol downgrade testing -- send intentionally non-conformant HTTP to observe server behavior

docs.title: HTTP/2 raw forwarding
docs.text:
For HTTP/2, raw mode operates on individual frames rather than the complete connection stream. When you provide raw bytes, the proxy:

  1. Parses the 9-byte frame headers to locate stream ID fields
  2. Rewrites stream IDs to match the upstream connection's allocated stream (connection-level frames with stream ID 0 are not rewritten)
  3. Forwards the frames as-is, preserving all other bytes including flags, padding, and payload

This means you can craft custom HEADERS, DATA, or other frame types while the proxy handles the stream multiplexing automatically.

docs.title: Using raw mode
docs.text:
Release with raw bytes (forward original wire bytes without HTTP normalization):

// intercept
{
  "action": "release",
  "params": {
    "intercept_id": "int-abc-123",
    "mode": "raw"
  }
}

Modify and forward with raw bytes (replace the entire payload):

// intercept
{
  "action": "modify_and_forward",
  "params": {
    "intercept_id": "int-abc-123",
    "mode": "raw",
    "raw_override_base64": "R0VUIC8gSFRUUC8xLjENCkhvc3Q6IGV4YW1wbGUuY29tDQoNCg=="
  }
}

The raw_override_base64 value is the Base64 encoding of the complete raw bytes you want sent on the wire. For HTTP/1.x, this is the full request including the request line, headers, and body. For HTTP/2, this is one or more serialized frames.

Note

Raw mode requires raw bytes to be available for the intercepted item. The response includes raw_bytes_available: true when this is the case.

docs.title: WebUI integration
docs.text: The intercept queue is also accessible through the Web UI, where you can visually inspect and act on queued items. The WebUI provides a hex dump editor and text editor for raw bytes editing. See WebUI Intercept for details.

docs.title: Inspect login requests
docs.text:
Intercept login requests to test different credential combinations in real time:

// configure
{
  "intercept_rules": {
    "add": [
      {
        "id": "login-intercept",
        "enabled": true,
        "direction": "request",
        "conditions": {
          "path_pattern": "/login",
          "methods": ["POST"]
        }
      }
    ]
  }
}

docs.title: Modify API responses
docs.text:
Intercept responses to test how the client handles different server behaviors:

// configure
{
  "intercept_rules": {
    "add": [
      {
        "id": "api-responses",
        "enabled": true,
        "direction": "response",
        "conditions": {
          "host_pattern": "api\\.target\\.com",
          "header_match": {"Content-Type": "application/json"}
        }
      }
    ]
  }
}

docs.title: Intercept by header
docs.text:
Intercept only requests with specific headers:

// configure
{
  "intercept_rules": {
    "add": [
      {
        "id": "auth-requests",
        "enabled": true,
        "direction": "request",
        "conditions": {
          "header_match": {"Authorization": "Bearer.*"}
        }
      }
    ]
  }
}

docs.text:

docs.title: Macros
docs.text: Macros let you define multi-step workflows that execute a sequence of HTTP requests with variable extraction, template expansion, and conditional logic. They are essential for testing authenticated flows, chained API operations, and any scenario requiring state between requests.

docs.title: Core concepts
docs.text:
A macro consists of:

  • Steps -- ordered HTTP requests based on recorded flows
  • KV Store -- a key-value store for passing data between steps via §variable§ templates
  • Extraction rules -- rules to extract values from responses into the KV Store
  • Guards -- conditions that control whether a step executes

docs.title: Defining a macro
docs.text:
Use the define_macro action to save a macro definition. If a macro with the same name exists, it is updated (upsert):

// macro
{
  "action": "define_macro",
  "params": {
    "name": "auth-flow",
    "description": "Login and get CSRF token",
    "steps": [
      {
        "id": "login",
        "flow_id": "recorded-login-flow",
        "override_body": "username=admin&password=§password§",
        "extract": [
          {
            "name": "session_cookie",
            "from": "response",
            "source": "header",
            "header_name": "Set-Cookie",
            "regex": "PHPSESSID=([^;]+)",
            "group": 1
          }
        ]
      },
      {
        "id": "get-csrf",
        "flow_id": "recorded-csrf-flow",
        "override_headers": {"Cookie": "PHPSESSID=§session_cookie§"},
        "extract": [
          {
            "name": "csrf_token",
            "from": "response",
            "source": "body",
            "regex": "name=\"csrf\" value=\"([^\"]+)\"",
            "group": 1
          }
        ]
      }
    ],
    "initial_vars": {"password": "admin123"}
  }
}

docs.title: Step definition
docs.text:
Each step specifies a recorded flow as a template and optional mutations:

Field Type Description id string Unique step identifier (required) flow_id string Recorded flow to use as template (required) override_method string Override HTTP method (supports §variable§ templates) override_url string Override request URL (supports §variable§ templates) override_headers object Header overrides (templates in values only; names match case-sensitively) override_body string Override request body (supports templates) on_error string Error handling: "abort" (default), "skip", "retry" retry_count integer Retry count when on_error is "retry" (default: 3) retry_delay_ms integer Delay between retries in ms (default: 1000) timeout_ms integer Step timeout in ms (default: 60000) extract array Value extraction rules when object Guard condition for conditional execution

docs.title: Variable extraction
docs.text: Extraction rules pull values from responses and store them in the KV Store for use in subsequent steps.

docs.title: Extraction sources
docs.text: Source Description header Extract from a response header (requires header_name) body Extract from the response body using regex body_json Extract from a JSON response using json_path status Extract the HTTP status code url Extract from the response URL (after redirects)

docs.title: Extraction from headers
docs.text:
{
  "name": "session_cookie",
  "from": "response",
  "source": "header",
  "header_name": "Set-Cookie",
  "regex": "PHPSESSID=([^;]+)",
  "group": 1
}

docs.title: Extraction from body with regex
docs.text:
{
  "name": "csrf_token",
  "from": "response",
  "source": "body",
  "regex": "name=\"csrf\" value=\"([^\"]+)\"",
  "group": 1
}

docs.title: Extraction from JSON body
docs.text:
{
  "name": "access_token",
  "from": "response",
  "source": "body_json",
  "json_path": "$.data.access_token"
}

docs.title: Extraction from status code
docs.text:
{
  "name": "login_status",
  "from": "response",
  "source": "status"
}

docs.title: Extraction options
docs.text: Field Type Description name string Variable name to store in KV Store (required) from string "request" or "response" (required) source string Extraction source (required) header_name string Header name (for header source) regex string Regex pattern (for header and body sources) group integer Capture group index (default: 0 = full match) json_path string JSON path (for body_json source) default string Default value if extraction fails required boolean Fail the step if extraction fails

docs.title: Template expansion
docs.text:
Use §variable§ syntax in override_method, override_url, override_headers (values), and override_body to reference KV Store values. These four fields are the only expansion sites -- extract and when are never expanded:

{
  "id": "api-call",
  "flow_id": "api-flow",
  "override_url": "https://api.target.com/v1/users/§user_id§",
  "override_headers": {
    "Authorization": "Bearer §access_token§",
    "Cookie": "session=§session_cookie§"
  },
  "override_body": "{\"csrf\": \"§csrf_token§\"}"
}

Variables are expanded at execution time, after any preceding step's extractions have populated the KV Store.

Values can be piped through encoders: §payload | url_encode§, §credentials | base64§. Available encoders are url_encode, base64, base64_decode, hex, html_encode, lower, upper, md5, and sha256. An unknown encoder fails the step.

Header names on HTTP/2 flows

An override_headers key replaces a recorded header only on a case-sensitive name match. HTTP/2 flows record lowercase header names, so write cookie instead of Cookie when the step's flow_id was captured over HTTP/2.

docs.title: Unresolved variable warnings
docs.text:
An unknown §variable§ is left literally on the wire, but yorishiro-proxy reports it instead of sending it silently:

  • At definition time -- define_macro returns warnings[] for every §name§ that is defined by neither initial_vars, a preceding step's extract, nor a reserved __ key. The macro is still saved; ignore the warning if you plan to supply the value through run_macro vars.
  • At run time -- run_macro re-checks each step against the live KV Store just before sending. An unresolved name sets the step's status to "warning", and step_results[*].warnings names the location plus the variable names that are available, which makes typos easy to spot.

Foreign syntaxes such as {{var}}, ${var}, and %var% are never expanded. They are sent literally (so template-injection payloads pass through unmodified) and also produce a step warning that suggests the §var§ rewrite.

docs.title: Guards (conditional execution)
docs.text:
Guards control whether a step executes based on conditions from a previous step's result:

{
  "id": "admin-action",
  "flow_id": "admin-flow",
  "when": {
    "step": "login",
    "status_code": 200,
    "body_match": "\"role\":\"admin\""
  }
}

docs.title: Guard fields
docs.text: Field Type Description step string Step ID to evaluate (must be a previous step) status_code integer Require exact status code match status_code_range [int, int] Require status code within range (inclusive) header_match object Header name-to-regex mapping (AND logic) body_match string Regex pattern to match in response body extracted_var string Require this KV Store variable to exist and be non-empty negate boolean Invert the guard condition

docs.title: Negated guard example
docs.text:
Skip a step if the login returned a 403:

{
  "id": "dashboard",
  "flow_id": "dashboard-flow",
  "when": {
    "step": "login",
    "status_code": 403,
    "negate": true
  }
}

docs.title: Running a macro
docs.text:
Execute a stored macro with optional runtime variable overrides:

// macro
{
  "action": "run_macro",
  "params": {
    "name": "auth-flow",
    "vars": {"password": "different-password"}
  }
}

Runtime vars take precedence over initial_vars defined in the macro.

The result includes:

  • status -- "completed", "error", or "timeout"
  • steps_executed -- number of steps that ran
  • kv_store -- final KV Store contents
  • step_results -- per-step status (completed, warning, skipped, error), status codes, durations, errors, and warnings

docs.title: Hook integration
docs.text:
Macros power the pre_macro / post_macro hooks on the typed fuzz tools (fuzz_http, fuzz_ws, fuzz_grpc, fuzz_raw). A hook references a stored macro by name and shares its KV Store with the fuzz variants.

// fuzz_http
{
  "flow_id": "target-flow",
  "headers": [
    {"name": "Cookie", "value": "PHPSESSID=§session_cookie§"}
  ],
  "positions": [
    {"path": "raw_query", "payloads": ["id=1", "id=2", "id=3"]}
  ],
  "pre_macro": {"name": "auth-flow", "scope": "job"},
  "post_macro": {
    "name": "log-response",
    "run_interval": "on_status",
    "status_codes": [401, 403]
  }
}

docs.title: Scopes
docs.text:
Scope Fires KV Store iteration (default) Around every variant Fresh per variant job Once before (pre) or after (post) the variant loop Shared by every variant

Job-scope extracts are copied into each variant's KV Store, so a single login can feed every variant.

docs.title: Run intervals
docs.text:
run_interval applies to scope="iteration" hooks only (combining it with scope="job" is rejected).

pre_macro:

Interval Description always Run before every variant (default) once Run only before the first variant every_n Run every N variants (requires n) on_error Run when the previous variant failed (transport error or HTTP status >= 400 on fuzz_http; see each tool for its own error rule)

post_macro:

Interval Description always Run after every variant (default) on_status Run when the response status matches status_codes on_match Run when the response matches the match_pattern regex

An iteration-scope post_macro receives the variant's response as reserved __response_* variables (for fuzz_http: __response_status, __response_body, __response_headers__<lower(name)>__). The key set differs per protocol -- see each fuzz tool's page.

docs.title: Error handling and overrides
docs.text:
• on_error: skip (default) skips the variant -- or the whole job for a job-scope pre_macro -- when the hook fails; abort stops the run; continue proceeds anyway.
  • vars: static string-to-string overrides injected into the hook's KV Store. Keys starting with __ are reserved and silently dropped.

docs.title: Retry policy
docs.text:
Steps can be configured with automatic retry on failure:

{
  "id": "flaky-api",
  "flow_id": "api-flow",
  "on_error": "retry",
  "retry_count": 3,
  "retry_delay_ms": 2000,
  "timeout_ms": 10000
}
Error handling Description abort Stop the macro on error (default) skip Skip the failed step and continue retry Retry the step up to retry_count times

docs.title: Deleting a macro
docs.text:
// macro
{
  "action": "delete_macro",
  "params": {"name": "auth-flow"}
}

docs.title: Practical example: login, token, API access
docs.text:
This example demonstrates a complete authentication flow:

// macro
{
  "action": "define_macro",
  "params": {
    "name": "full-auth-flow",
    "description": "Login, extract token, access protected API",
    "steps": [
      {
        "id": "login",
        "flow_id": "login-flow-id",
        "override_body": "{\"username\":\"§username§\",\"password\":\"§password§\"}",
        "extract": [
          {
            "name": "access_token",
            "from": "response",
            "source": "body_json",
            "json_path": "$.data.access_token",
            "required": true
          },
          {
            "name": "refresh_token",
            "from": "response",
            "source": "body_json",
            "json_path": "$.data.refresh_token"
          }
        ]
      },
      {
        "id": "get-profile",
        "flow_id": "profile-flow-id",
        "override_headers": {
          "Authorization": "Bearer §access_token§"
        },
        "when": {
          "step": "login",
          "status_code_range": [200, 299]
        },
        "extract": [
          {
            "name": "user_id",
            "from": "response",
            "source": "body_json",
            "json_path": "$.data.id"
          }
        ]
      },
      {
        "id": "admin-action",
        "flow_id": "admin-flow-id",
        "override_url": "https://api.target.com/admin/users/§user_id§",
        "override_headers": {
          "Authorization": "Bearer §access_token§"
        },
        "when": {
          "step": "get-profile",
          "extracted_var": "user_id"
        }
      }
    ],
    "initial_vars": {
      "username": "admin",
      "password": "admin123"
    },
    "macro_timeout_ms": 60000
  }
}

docs.text:
• Macro tool reference -- MCP tool parameter reference
  • Fuzzer -- pre_macro / post_macro hooks for fuzz campaigns
  • Resender -- Single request resend

docs.title: Rate limits and diagnostic budgets
docs.text: Rate limits and diagnostic budgets control how aggressively the proxy sends requests. Rate limits cap the requests per second, while budgets cap the total number of requests or session duration. Both use the two-layer architecture (Policy + Agent) for safe operation.

docs.title: Global RPS
docs.text:
Limit the total number of requests per second across all hosts:

// security
{
  "action": "set_rate_limits",
  "params": {
    "max_requests_per_second": 10
  }
}

docs.title: Per-host RPS
docs.text:
Limit requests per second to each individual host:

// security
{
  "action": "set_rate_limits",
  "params": {
    "max_requests_per_host_per_second": 5
  }
}

docs.title: Combined limits
docs.text:
Set both global and per-host limits:

// security
{
  "action": "set_rate_limits",
  "params": {
    "max_requests_per_second": 50,
    "max_requests_per_host_per_second": 10
  }
}

docs.title: Clearing limits
docs.text:
Set a limit to 0 to remove it. Omitted fields also reset to 0 (no limit) because set_rate_limits uses full-replace semantics:

// security
{
  "action": "set_rate_limits",
  "params": {
    "max_requests_per_second": 0,
    "max_requests_per_host_per_second": 0
  }
}

docs.title: Rate limit enforcement
docs.text: Requests that exceed rate limits receive a 429 Too Many Requests response with an X-Blocked-By: rate_limit header.

docs.title: Diagnostic budgets
docs.text: Budgets limit the total scope of a testing session by capping either the number of requests or the duration.

docs.title: Request budget
docs.text:
Limit the total number of requests:

// security
{
  "action": "set_budget",
  "params": {
    "max_total_requests": 1000
  }
}

docs.title: Duration budget
docs.text:
Limit the session duration using Go duration strings:

// security
{
  "action": "set_budget",
  "params": {
    "max_duration": "30m"
  }
}

Supported duration formats: "30m", "1h", "2h30m", "0s" (no limit).

docs.title: Combined budgets
docs.text:
// security
{
  "action": "set_budget",
  "params": {
    "max_total_requests": 5000,
    "max_duration": "2h"
  }
}

docs.title: Budget exhaustion
docs.text:
When a budget is exhausted, the proxy automatically stops accepting new requests. The stop_reason field in the budget status indicates why:

  • "max_total_requests exceeded"
  • "max_duration exceeded"

docs.title: Two-layer architecture
docs.text: Rate limits and budgets use the same two-layer design as Target scope:

docs.title: Policy layer
docs.text: Set at startup from the config file's target_scope_policy section or the -target-policy-file. Defines the upper bounds that the agent cannot exceed. The agent cannot change it; only the operator can replace it at runtime with a SIGHUP reload (see Reloading the Policy layer). A reload does not reset the request counter, and re-arms the duration limit against the new value from the original session start.

docs.title: Agent layer
docs.text: Controlled by the AI agent via the security tool. Can set limits that are equal to or stricter than Policy limits, but never more permissive.

docs.title: Effective values
docs.text: The effective limit is always the stricter of the two layers. For example, if the Policy sets 50 RPS and the Agent sets 10 RPS, the effective limit is 10 RPS.

docs.title: Rate limits
docs.text:
// security
{
  "action": "get_rate_limits"
}

Response:

{
  "policy": {
    "max_requests_per_second": 50,
    "max_requests_per_host_per_second": 20
  },
  "agent": {
    "max_requests_per_second": 10,
    "max_requests_per_host_per_second": 5
  },
  "effective": {
    "max_requests_per_second": 10,
    "max_requests_per_host_per_second": 5
  }
}

docs.title: Budget status
docs.text:
// security
{
  "action": "get_budget"
}

Response:

{
  "policy": {
    "max_total_requests": 5000,
    "max_duration": "2h0m0s"
  },
  "agent": {
    "max_total_requests": 1000,
    "max_duration": "30m0s"
  },
  "effective": {
    "max_total_requests": 1000,
    "max_duration": "30m0s"
  },
  "request_count": 142,
  "stop_reason": ""
}

docs.title: Budget via configure tool
docs.text:
You can also set budgets using the configure tool, which uses merge semantics by default (only update provided fields, keep others unchanged):

// configure
{
  "budget": {
    "max_total_requests": 1000,
    "max_duration": "30m"
  }
}

This differs from the security tool's set_budget action, which uses full-replace semantics (omitted fields reset to 0).

docs.title: Config file setup
docs.text:
Set Policy layer limits in the config file's target_scope_policy section (or at the top level of a -target-policy-file):

{
  "target_scope_policy": {
    "rate_limits": {
      "max_requests_per_second": 50,
      "max_requests_per_host_per_second": 20
    },
    "budget": {
      "max_total_requests": 10000,
      "max_duration": "4h"
    }
  }
}

Values must be >= 0 (0 means unlimited). A negative value is rejected at load instead of silently meaning "unlimited".

docs.title: Conservative scanning
docs.text:
For initial reconnaissance with minimal impact:

// security
{
  "action": "set_rate_limits",
  "params": {
    "max_requests_per_second": 5,
    "max_requests_per_host_per_second": 2
  }
}

// security
{
  "action": "set_budget",
  "params": {
    "max_total_requests": 500,
    "max_duration": "15m"
  }
}

docs.title: Intensive fuzzing
docs.text:
For targeted fuzzing within operator-approved limits:

// security
{
  "action": "set_rate_limits",
  "params": {
    "max_requests_per_second": 100,
    "max_requests_per_host_per_second": 50
  }
}

docs.title: Resender
docs.text: The resender lets you replay recorded proxy requests with optional mutations. You can override the method, URL, headers, and body, apply JSON patches or regex replacements, and resend raw bytes for protocol-level testing. Each protocol has its own typed sibling tool.

docs.title: Tools overview
docs.text: Tool Description resend_http Resend an HTTP/1.x or HTTP/2 request with typed HTTPMessage fields resend_ws Resend a single WebSocket frame resend_grpc Resend a gRPC unary RPC resend_raw Resend raw bytes over TCP/TLS with byte-level patches

docs.title: Resending with overrides
docs.text: The resend_http tool replays a recorded HTTP flow and lets you override any part of the request. The original flow is not modified; a new stream is created with the result.

docs.title: Method override
docs.text:
Change the HTTP method of the request:

// resend_http
{
  "flow_id": "abc-123",
  "method": "PUT"
}

docs.title: URL override
docs.text:
Redirect the request to a different path or authority. Set the components individually:

// resend_http
{
  "flow_id": "abc-123",
  "scheme": "https",
  "authority": "staging.target.com",
  "path": "/api/v2/users"
}

docs.title: Header mutations
docs.text:
Supplying headers replaces the recorded send's full ordered header list. To change a single header, recover the recorded list (e.g. via query), edit the entry, and pass the full list back:

// resend_http
{
  "flow_id": "abc-123",
  "headers": [
    {"name": "Content-Type", "value": "application/json"},
    {"name": "X-Custom", "value": "value1"},
    {"name": "X-Custom", "value": "value2"}
  ]
}

The list preserves wire case, order, and duplicates. To remove a header, simply omit it from the supplied list. Header names and values containing CR/LF are rejected (CWE-113 guard).

docs.title: Body override
docs.text:
Replace the entire request body with text or Base64-encoded binary data:

// resend_http
{
  "flow_id": "abc-123",
  "body": "{\"username\": \"admin\", \"role\": \"superuser\"}"
}

For binary data, set body_encoding to "base64":

// resend_http
{
  "flow_id": "abc-123",
  "body": "SGVsbG8gV29ybGQ=",
  "body_encoding": "base64"
}

To send an explicitly empty body, set "body_set": true (omitting body alone inherits the recorded body). When body is set it replaces the recorded body before body_patches are applied.

docs.title: JSON patches
docs.text:
For surgical modifications to JSON bodies, use body_patches with json_path. The path uses simplified dot notation ($.key1.key2):

// resend_http
{
  "flow_id": "abc-123",
  "body_patches": [
    {"json_path": "$.user.role", "value": "admin"},
    {"json_path": "$.user.active", "value": true},
    {"json_path": "$.settings.limit", "value": 9999}
  ]
}

JSON path limitations

The JSON path parser supports dot notation only ($.key1.key2.key3). Array index notation is not supported. The $ prefix is optional.

docs.title: Regex body patches
docs.text:
For text-based modifications, use body_patches with regex and replace. Capture group references ($1, $2) are supported:

// resend_http
{
  "flow_id": "abc-123",
  "body_patches": [
    {"regex": "csrf_token=[^&]+", "replace": "csrf_token=injected_value"},
    {"regex": "(role=)(user)", "replace": "${1}admin"}
  ]
}

docs.title: Encoding chains
docs.text:
Both JSON and regex patches support an encoding array that applies codec transformations to the patch value before applying. Codecs are applied in pipeline order:

// resend_http
{
  "flow_id": "abc-123",
  "body_patches": [
    {
      "json_path": "$.token",
      "value": "<script>alert(1)</script>",
      "encoding": ["url_encode_query", "base64"]
    }
  ]
}

Available codecs: base64, base64url, url_encode_query, url_encode_path, url_encode_full, double_url_encode, hex, html_entity, html_escape, unicode_escape, md5, sha256, lower, upper.

Maximum chain length is 10 codecs.

docs.title: Body mutation priority
docs.text:
The body is resolved in this priority order:

  1. body (full replacement; or body_set: true to force empty)
  2. body_patches (partial modifications)
  3. Original body from the recorded flow

docs.title: Raw bytes resend
docs.text:
The resend_raw tool sends the raw bytes from a recorded flow over a freshly dialled TCP/TLS connection. This is useful for testing HTTP request smuggling, malformed requests, or protocol-level vulnerabilities. target_addr (host:port) is required -- raw is protocol-agnostic, so there is no defaulting.

// resend_raw
{
  "flow_id": "abc-123",
  "target_addr": "target.com:443",
  "use_tls": true
}

docs.title: Raw byte patches
docs.text:
You can modify raw bytes with offset-based patches:

// resend_raw
{
  "flow_id": "abc-123",
  "target_addr": "target.com:443",
  "use_tls": true,
  "patches": [
    {"offset": 0, "data": "R0VU", "data_encoding": "base64"}
  ]
}

Each patch overwrites bytes at the given zero-based offset. data_encoding defaults to "text" for ASCII edits:

// resend_raw
{
  "flow_id": "abc-123",
  "target_addr": "target.com:80",
  "patches": [
    {"offset": 0, "data": "POST"}
  ]
}

Find/replace patch modes from the legacy tool are no longer supported -- compute offsets client-side from the recovered bytes (available via query).

You can also fully replace the bytes with override_bytes (paired with override_bytes_encoding):

// resend_raw
{
  "flow_id": "abc-123",
  "target_addr": "target.com:80",
  "override_bytes": "R0VUIC8gSFRUUC8xLjENCkhvc3Q6IGV4YW1wbGUuY29tDQoNCg==",
  "override_bytes_encoding": "base64"
}

docs.title: Raw TCP replay
docs.text:
To replay a raw TCP flow as-is, use resend_raw without overrides. Each call records a new stream containing the resend's send and received bytechunk flows:

// resend_raw
{
  "flow_id": "tcp-flow-456",
  "target_addr": "db.target.com:3306",
  "use_tls": false,
  "tag": "tcp-replay-test"
}

docs.title: Multi-protocol support
docs.text:
Each protocol has its own typed resend tool:

Protocol Tool HTTP/1.x and HTTP/2 resend_http WebSocket resend_ws gRPC resend_grpc Raw TCP / TLS resend_raw

docs.title: HTTP/2 resend
docs.text:
A flow recorded over HTTP/2 is resent over HTTP/2 by default: h2 (TLS, ALPN) for https, h2c (prior knowledge) for http. Use http_version to choose explicitly ("http/1.1", "h2", or "h2c"). If the upstream does not negotiate h2, the call fails with an error naming the negotiated ALPN instead of silently falling back. See Wire protocol.

// resend_http
{
  "flow_id": "h2-flow-123",
  "http_version": "http/1.1"
}

For resend_grpc, TLS is decided from the transport the recorded flow actually used, not from the declared :scheme.

docs.title: WebSocket resend
docs.text:
For WebSocket flows, use resend_ws. Each call dials a fresh upstream, performs the upgrade dance, sends one frame, and records the response:

// resend_ws
{
  "flow_id": "ws-flow-123",
  "opcode": "text",
  "payload": "{\"action\":\"ping\"}"
}

To send from scratch (no recorded flow), supply target_addr, scheme, and path:

// resend_ws
{
  "target_addr": "ws.target.com:443",
  "scheme": "wss",
  "path": "/socket",
  "opcode": "binary",
  "payload": "AAECAw==",
  "body_encoding": "base64"
}

docs.title: Additional options
docs.text:
Parameter Type Description override_host string (HTTP) Redirect the dial target while preserving the request's Host / :authority (must be host:port) target_addr string (WS / raw) Upstream host:port for the dial timeout_ms integer Per-call timeout in milliseconds (default: 30000) tag string Tag stored on the new stream's Tags map upstream_proxy object (HTTP) Route this call through an upstream proxy. url_template supports §__nonce§ (fresh UUID per call) for residential-proxy IP switching. See Upstream proxy

follow_redirects is no longer auto-followed -- chase redirects from the client side by inspecting the response and issuing a new resend.

docs.title: Hooks integration
docs.text: Pre/post macro hooks for individual resend calls have been removed in favor of the streamlined per-protocol pipeline (PluginStepPost -> RecordStep). To run a macro before or after a resend, invoke the macro tool independently and stitch the calls from the client side. See Macros for the standalone macro execution model.

docs.title: Authentication testing
docs.text:
Resend a login request with different credentials to test for weak password policies:

// resend_http
{
  "flow_id": "login-flow-id",
  "body_patches": [
    {"json_path": "$.password", "value": "admin123"}
  ]
}

docs.title: Parameter tampering
docs.text:
Modify a recorded API request to test for authorization bypass:

// resend_http
{
  "flow_id": "api-flow-id",
  "body_patches": [
    {"json_path": "$.user_id", "value": 1},
    {"json_path": "$.role", "value": "admin"}
  ],
  "tag": "idor-test"
}

docs.title: HTTP request smuggling
docs.text:
Use resend_raw with offset patches to test for request smuggling. Compute offsets from the recovered bytes (available via query) and patch the relevant header bytes:

// resend_raw
{
  "flow_id": "abc-123",
  "target_addr": "target.com:80",
  "patches": [
    {"offset": 64, "data": "Transfer-Encoding: chunked\r\n\r\n"}
  ]
}

docs.title: SafetyFilter
docs.text:
SafetyFilter is a two-part content filtering system that prevents destructive payloads from being sent to target systems (Input Filter) and protects sensitive information from being exposed to AI agents (Output Filter). SafetyFilter rules are part of the Policy layer and cannot be modified at runtime.

SafetyFilter is envelope-native: rules operate on the typed Envelope.Message and the ordered []envelope.KeyValue headers. The Pipeline SafetyStep dispatches via a type-switch on env.Message to per-protocol safety engines (internal/rules/http, internal/rules/ws, internal/rules/grpc); each engine reuses the regex / preset machinery in internal/safety for body, URL, query, and header matching.

docs.title: Input filter
docs.text: The Input Filter inspects outgoing Send-direction messages (body, URL, query string, headers) against regex rules and blocks or logs matches before the message reaches the target. Receive-direction messages always pass through — the Input Filter is Send-only.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
When a message is about to be sent (via the proxy data path, resend, fuzz, macro, or intercept modify_and_forward), the Input Filter:

  1. Evaluates the body, URL, query string, and headers against all input rules
  2. If a rule matches with block action, the message is rejected with an error
  3. If a rule matches with log_only action, the match is logged but the message proceeds

docs.title: Built-in presets
docs.text: Preset Rules Description destructive-sql 6 rules DROP TABLE/DATABASE/INDEX/VIEW/SCHEMA, TRUNCATE TABLE, DELETE without WHERE, UPDATE WHERE 1=1, ALTER TABLE DROP, xp_ stored procedures destructive-os-command 5 rules rm -rf, shutdown/reboot/halt/poweroff, mkfs, dd if=, Windows format

docs.title: Input targets
docs.text: Target Description body Request body content url Full URL string query Query string portion of the URL header Individual header values (use header:Name for specific headers) headers All header values concatenated

docs.title: Blocked response
docs.text:
When the Input Filter blocks a request at the proxy layer:

  • Status: 403 Forbidden
  • Header: X-Block-Reason: safety_filter
  • Body: JSON with violation details (rule ID, rule name, match location)

When it blocks a native gRPC call at the proxy layer, the client receives a Trailers-Only response instead of hanging until its deadline:

  • grpc-status: 7 (PERMISSION_DENIED)
  • grpc-message: blocked by safety_filter
  • Trailers: server: yorishiro-proxy and x-yorishiro-matched-rules

The upstream stream, if already opened, is closed. gRPC-Web and WebSocket messages are dropped.

When it blocks an MCP tool operation:

  • MCP error response with violation details

The matched fragment is never written to the log in clear text: the log line carries a truncated SHA-256 digest and the byte length, so a match on an Authorization or Cookie header does not leak the secret.

docs.title: gRPC targets
docs.text: For a gRPC call, the url target covers the :path (/package.Service/Method) and the query target covers any query component, so the built-in presets also fire on the RPC target, not just on message payloads.

docs.title: Output filter
docs.text: The Output Filter prevents sensitive information (PII) from being exposed to AI agents. It inspects response bodies and headers against regex rules and masks matching content before returning data to the agent.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. MCP tool layer: Query results, resend responses, fuzz results, intercept queue entries, and export data are masked before returning to the AI agent
  2. Wire untouched: Traffic relayed to the client and the next hop is never modified by the Output Filter
  3. Raw data preserved: The Flow Store always contains the original unmasked data for human review via the Web UI

docs.title: Built-in PII presets
docs.text: Preset Rules Description credit-card 2 rules Credit card numbers in separated (1234-5678-9012-3456) and continuous (1234567890123456) formats japan-my-number 1 rule Japanese My Number (12-digit individual number) with check digit validation email 1 rule Email addresses (user@example.com) japan-phone 2 rules Japanese phone numbers in mobile (090-1234-5678) and landline (03-1234-5678) formats

docs.title: Validators
docs.text:
Some presets use validator functions for additional verification beyond regex matching, reducing false positives:

  • credit-card (continuous): Luhn algorithm check -- only masks digit sequences that pass the Luhn checksum
  • japan-my-number: Check digit validation -- only masks 12-digit sequences with a valid My Number check digit

docs.title: Output actions
docs.text: Action Description mask Replace matched content with the replacement string log_only Log the match but return data unmodified

docs.title: Replacement strings
docs.text:
Replacement strings support regex capture group references:

Syntax Description [MASKED:credit_card] Static replacement $1 First capture group ${name} Named capture group

docs.title: Two-layer architecture
docs.text:
Like Target scope and Rate limits, SafetyFilter uses the Policy + Agent two-layer architecture:

  • Policy layer: SafetyFilter rules are defined in the config file and are immutable at runtime
  • Agent layer: AI agents can view rules via get_safety_filter but cannot modify them

This ensures that safety boundaries remain enforced regardless of agent behavior.

docs.title: Enforcement points
docs.text:
The Input Filter is enforced at every point where the proxy sends data to external targets:

Tool Enforcement Proxy data path SafetyStep runs on every Send-direction envelope, before transform and downstream encode resend_http / resend_ws / resend_grpc Typed message checked before sending resend_raw Raw bytes checked before sending fuzz_http / fuzz_ws / fuzz_grpc / fuzz_raw Template envelope checked at start; each expanded payload checked before sending (after the per-variant target scope check) macro Each step's outbound message checked before sending intercept Every release re-checks target scope, then modify_and_forward envelopes are re-checked by the Input Filter (USK-702)

docs.title: Re-check at HoldQueue release
docs.text:
When an operator holds a message via Intercept and chooses modify-and-forward, the user-modified envelope is re-evaluated by SafetyStep before being released downstream. The original held envelope already passed SafetyStep at hold time (the canonical chain runs Safety → Intercept), but modify_and_forward lets the operator inject content that would bypass that gate — for example, replacing a benign body with a DROP TABLE payload.

The re-check uses the same per-protocol engine as the inline check, so coverage is identical for HTTP, WebSocket, and gRPC. If the modified envelope trips the Input Filter, the release is rejected and the envelope is dropped.

The Output Filter is enforced at every point where data is returned to the AI agent:

Source Enforcement query results Flow data masked in query output resend results Response body and headers masked fuzz results Response data masked export data Inline export data masked

docs.title: Viewing current rules
docs.text:
Use the security tool to view the current SafetyFilter configuration:

// security
{
  "action": "get_safety_filter"
}

Response:

{
  "enabled": true,
  "input_rules": [
    {
      "id": "destructive-sql:drop",
      "name": "DROP statement",
      "pattern": "(compiled regex)",
      "targets": ["body", "url", "query"],
      "action": "block",
      "category": "destructive-sql"
    }
  ],
  "output_rules": [
    {
      "id": "credit-card:separated",
      "name": "Credit card (separated)",
      "pattern": "(compiled regex)",
      "targets": ["body"],
      "action": "mask",
      "replacement": "[MASKED:credit_card]",
      "category": "credit-card"
    }
  ],
  "immutable": true
}

docs.title: Custom rules
docs.text: Custom rules are defined in the config file.

docs.title: Custom input rule
docs.text:
{
  "id": "custom-api",
  "name": "Dangerous API endpoint",
  "pattern": "(?i)/api/v[0-9]+/(delete-all|reset)",
  "targets": ["url"]
}

docs.title: Custom output rule
docs.text:
{
  "id": "custom-api-key",
  "name": "API key pattern",
  "pattern": "(sk-[a-zA-Z0-9]{32,})",
  "targets": ["body"],
  "action": "mask",
  "replacement": "[MASKED:api_key]"
}

docs.title: Target scope
docs.text:
Target scope controls which hosts and URLs the proxy is allowed to send requests to. It uses a two-layer architecture that separates policy-level controls (set by the operator) from agent-level controls (set by the AI agent at runtime).

Target scope is the only scope mechanism in the proxy. It is enforced by HostScopeStep at the head of the canonical Pipeline chain (HostScope → HTTPScope → Budget → Safety → PluginPre → Intercept → Transform → PluginPost → Record), so connections targeting a denied host are filtered before any other Step runs. The check uses Envelope.Context.TargetHost (populated from the CONNECT or SOCKS5 target) and never inspects the typed Message.

docs.title: Policy layer
docs.text: The Policy layer is set at startup from -target-policy-file, or else the config file's target_scope_policy section. No MCP tool can modify it; only the operator can replace it at runtime by sending SIGHUP (see Reloading the Policy layer). It defines the upper boundary for what the agent can access.

docs.title: Agent layer
docs.text: The Agent layer is controlled by the AI agent via the security tool. It can further restrict access within the Policy layer boundaries, but cannot expand beyond them.

docs.title: Design rationale
docs.text:
This separation ensures that:

  • Operators define the maximum scope of testing (Policy layer)
  • AI agents can self-restrict within that scope (Agent layer)
  • Safety is enforced even if the agent attempts to bypass restrictions

docs.title: Evaluation order
docs.text:
When a request URL is checked against target scope:

  1. Policy denies -- always block (highest priority)
  2. Agent denies -- block
  3. Policy allows (if any) -- target must match at least one, otherwise block
  4. Agent allows (if any) -- target must match at least one, otherwise block
  5. All checks passed -- allow

The priority order is: deny > allow, and within each type: policy > agent.

When neither layer has rules, all targets are permitted (open mode).

docs.title: Rule definition
docs.text:
Each target rule specifies:

Field Type Description hostname string Exact name, wildcard *.example.com, IPv4 literal, or IPv6 literal (bare ::1 or bracketed [::1]). Required for Agent layer rules; a Policy layer rule may omit it to match any host ports array of int Match specific ports, 1-65535 (empty = all ports) path_prefix string Literal, case-sensitive URL path prefix. Must start with / (empty = all paths) schemes array of string http (plaintext) or https (TLS), case-insensitive (empty = both)

All specified fields must match for a rule to apply (AND logic).

docs.title: Rule validation
docs.text:
Both layers validate rules with the same checks. Because rules use AND logic, a condition that can never match makes the whole rule match nothing — for a deny rule, that silently disables it. Such rules are rejected instead:

Field Rejected Write instead hostname internal.corp. (trailing dot), host:443, https://host, *, *.10.0.0.1 (wildcard over an IP) internal.corp, host + ports, a bare IP path_prefix /api/*, admin, /search?q= /api/, /admin, /search schemes ws, wss, tcp, "" http / https, or omit

A Policy layer that fails validation stops the server at startup (or is rejected on reload). An Agent layer rule that fails is rejected by the security tool.

docs.title: Schemes mean transport confidentiality
docs.text:
schemes selects plaintext (http) versus TLS (https) — it is not an application-protocol name. WebSocket traffic maps ws to http and wss to https; raw TCP and gRPC map their TLS state the same way. A CONNECT tunnel is scoped as https regardless of what it carries.

SOCKS5 is the exception: the scope check runs before any tunnel byte is observed, so a SOCKS5 target has no scheme and does not match rules that carry schemes. Scope SOCKS5 targets by hostname and ports.

docs.title: IPv6 literals
docs.text: "::1", "[::1]", and "0:0::1" are the same rule: hosts are compared in canonical form. A zone-qualified target such as [fe80::1%eth0] does not match a zone-less rule.

docs.title: Wildcard hostnames
docs.text:
Use *.example.com to match subdomains. This matches sub.example.com but not example.com itself:

{"hostname": "*.target.com"}

docs.title: Config file policy setup
docs.text:
Set Policy layer rules in the config file:

{
  "target_scope_policy": {
    "allows": [
      {"hostname": "*.target.com"},
      {"hostname": "api.partner.com", "ports": [443], "schemes": ["https"]}
    ],
    "denies": [
      {"hostname": "*.internal.corp"},
      {"hostname": "admin.target.com"}
    ]
  }
}

Policy rules are loaded at startup and cannot be changed by the agent.

docs.title: Reloading the Policy layer
docs.text:
You can replace the running Policy layer — allows, denies, rate_limits, and budget together — without restarting. Edit the policy source and send the server SIGHUP (Unix only):

kill -HUP "$(pgrep -f 'yorishiro-proxy server')"
  • Requires a policy source. The handler is installed only when the server was started with -target-policy-file or -config, and only after the boot policy loads (log line target scope policy reload enabled). Otherwise SIGHUP terminates the process.
  • Full replacement. Reloading is equivalent to starting with that file. A section omitted from the new file (for example rate_limits) is cleared. Only the policy is reloaded; other config sections are not.
  • Atomic. The file is fully validated first. Malformed JSON, an invalid rule, or a negative limit rejects the whole reload, keeps the previous policy, and logs target scope policy reload rejected; previous policy retained.
  • Prefer -target-policy-file for live edits. The dedicated policy file is decoded strictly, so a misspelled key such as denys rejects the reload. The -config source is decoded leniently, so a typo there can reload as "no policy". When a reload removes every allow and deny rule, a warning is logged — check for it.
  • Applies to in-flight work. Live connections that the new policy denies are closed, held intercepts are re-checked on release, and running fuzz jobs re-check every variant. A deny that only names a path_prefix closes no connection; it is enforced per request.
  • Budget. The request counter is not reset; the duration limit is re-armed against the new value, measured from the original session start.
  • Audit. A successful reload is logged with the source path, file SHA-256, and rule counts. get_target_scope reports the policy's source and loaded_at.

Closing the terminal

With a policy source configured, closing the terminal that launched the server also sends SIGHUP and reloads instead of stopping the server. Stop it with SIGINT or SIGTERM.

docs.title: Set agent scope (full replace)
docs.text:
Replace all Agent layer rules:

// security
{
  "action": "set_target_scope",
  "params": {
    "allows": [
      {"hostname": "api.target.com", "ports": [443], "schemes": ["https"]},
      {"hostname": "*.target.com"}
    ],
    "denies": [
      {"hostname": "admin.target.com"}
    ]
  }
}

Use empty arrays to clear all agent rules:

// security
{
  "action": "set_target_scope",
  "params": {
    "allows": [],
    "denies": []
  }
}

Policy boundary enforcement

Agent allow rules must fall within the Policy allow boundary. If any agent allow rule is outside the policy scope, the entire operation is rejected.

docs.title: Update agent scope (incremental)
docs.text:
Apply incremental changes to Agent layer rules:

// security
{
  "action": "update_target_scope",
  "params": {
    "add_allows": [{"hostname": "new-api.target.com"}],
    "remove_allows": [{"hostname": "old-api.target.com"}],
    "add_denies": [{"hostname": "staging.target.com"}]
  }
}

Policy deny protection

You cannot remove Policy deny rules via remove_denies. Attempting to do so returns an error because policy rules are immutable.

docs.title: View current scope
docs.text:
// security
{
  "action": "get_target_scope"
}

Returns both Policy and Agent layer rules with the enforcement mode:

{
  "policy": {
    "allows": [{"hostname": "*.target.com"}],
    "denies": [{"hostname": "*.internal.corp"}],
    "source": "config file",
    "loaded_at": "2026-10-16T09:30:00Z",
    "immutable": true
  },
  "agent": {
    "allows": [{"hostname": "api.target.com"}],
    "denies": [{"hostname": "admin.target.com"}]
  },
  "effective_mode": "enforcing"
}

docs.title: URL test
docs.text:
Test a URL against current rules without making a request:

// security
{
  "action": "test_target",
  "params": {
    "url": "https://api.target.com/v1/users"
  }
}

The response tells you:

  • Whether the URL is allowed
  • Which layer made the decision
  • Which rule matched
  • The parsed URL components that were evaluated
{
  "allowed": true,
  "reason": "",
  "layer": "agent",
  "matched_rule": {"hostname": "api.target.com"},
  "tested_target": {
    "hostname": "api.target.com",
    "port": 443,
    "scheme": "https",
    "path": "/v1/users"
  }
}

docs.title: Enforcement modes
docs.text: Mode Description open No rules configured in either layer; all targets permitted enforcing At least one rule exists; targets are checked against rules

docs.title: Where target scope is enforced
docs.text:
Target scope is checked at multiple points:

  • Connection gates -- CONNECT, SOCKS5, and plain-HTTP forward connections are checked on admission, and re-checked whenever the scope changes; connections that would no longer be admitted are closed
  • Proxy data path -- HostScopeStep and HTTPScopeStep run on every Send-direction envelope flowing through the Pipeline, before any other Step
  • resend_http / resend_ws / resend_grpc -- before sending and after URL override
  • resend_raw -- before connecting to the target address
  • fuzz_http / fuzz_ws / fuzz_grpc / fuzz_raw -- on the template envelope, and again for every variant on the mutated message, so a scope change during a run stops the remaining variants
  • macro -- on each step's URL before execution and at send time after template expansion
  • intercept -- on every release (manual, timeout auto-release, and modify_and_forward), against the envelope about to be forwarded

This multi-point enforcement prevents SSRF via payload injection or template expansion.

docs.title: Deny symptoms
docs.text: Path What the client sees HTTPS via CONNECT tunnel 200 Connection Established (the tunnel acknowledgement), then the connection closes and the inner TLS handshake fails with EOF Plain-HTTP forward proxy 403 Forbidden with body yorishiro-proxy: target blocked by scope MCP tool request (resend_*, fuzz_*, macro) MCP error with the violation reason (fuzz records it as an error row and continues) Intercept release The intercept call succeeds; the forwarded HTTP request gets 403 with {"error":"blocked by target_scope","blocked_by":"target_scope"}, a WebSocket / gRPC message is dropped, and the block is recorded as a flow with blocked_by: target_scope

docs.title: CA certificate
docs.text: yorishiro-proxy performs HTTPS interception (MITM) by dynamically generating server certificates signed by its own CA. To inspect HTTPS traffic, you must install this CA certificate in your operating system or browser trust store.

docs.title: Automatic generation
docs.text:
On first startup, the CA certificate is automatically generated and saved to:

~/.yorishiro-proxy/ca/ca.crt   (certificate)
~/.yorishiro-proxy/ca/ca.key   (private key)

No manual action is required to generate the CA -- it is created the first time yorishiro-proxy runs.

Tip

Running yorishiro-proxy install ca --trust generates the CA certificate and registers it in your OS trust store automatically. On Linux it additionally registers the CA into the per-user NSSDB so Chromium and Firefox trust intercepted traffic out of the box (USK-857). You can skip the manual steps below.

docs.title: Check the CA certificate path
docs.text:
Use the query tool to confirm the CA certificate location:

// query
{"resource": "ca_cert"}

The response includes cert_path (file path) and fingerprint (SHA-256 hash) fields.

docs.title: OS-specific installation
docs.text:
macOSLinuxWindows 
sudo security add-trusted-cert -d -r trustRoot \
  -k /Library/Keychains/System.keychain \
  ~/.yorishiro-proxy/ca/ca.crt

sudo cp ~/.yorishiro-proxy/ca/ca.crt \
  /usr/local/share/ca-certificates/yorishiro-proxy.crt
sudo update-ca-certificates

Chromium and Firefox on Linux read their own per-user NSSDB rather than the OS trust store. yorishiro-proxy install ca --trust registers the CA there automatically (USK-857). If you installed the CA manually instead, register it explicitly with certutil:

mkdir -p "$HOME/.pki/nssdb"
certutil -d sql:"$HOME/.pki/nssdb" \
  -A -t "C,," -n "yorishiro-proxy" \
  -i ~/.yorishiro-proxy/ca/ca.crt

certutil is provided by libnss3-tools on Debian/Ubuntu and nss-tools on Fedora/RHEL.

Run the following command in an Administrator command prompt:

certutil -addstore "Root" %USERPROFILE%\.yorishiro-proxy\ca\ca.crt

docs.title: Alternative: skip CA installation with playwright-cli
docs.text:
If you are using playwright-cli for browser automation, you can skip CA certificate installation by enabling ignoreHTTPSErrors in the playwright configuration. This tells the browser to accept any certificate without verification.

Create .playwright/cli.config.json in your project root:

{
  "browser": {
    "browserName": "chromium",
    "launchOptions": {
      "channel": "chromium",
      "proxy": {
        "server": "http://127.0.0.1:8080"
      }
    },
    "contextOptions": {
      "ignoreHTTPSErrors": true
    }
  }
}

With this configuration, playwright-cli will route traffic through the proxy and accept yorishiro-proxy's dynamically generated certificates without needing to install the CA in the OS trust store.

docs.title: Ephemeral CA
docs.text:
If you do not want to persist the CA certificate to disk, use the -ca-ephemeral flag:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "yorishiro-proxy": {
      "command": "/path/to/bin/yorishiro-proxy",
      "args": ["server", "-stdio-mcp", "-ca-ephemeral"]
    }
  }
}

An ephemeral CA is generated in memory on each launch. This is useful for testing, but the certificate changes on every restart, so you cannot install it in a trust store.

docs.text:

  • HTTPS MITM -- how HTTPS interception works
  • TLS configuration -- advanced TLS settings

docs.title: First capture
docs.text: This guide walks you through capturing your first HTTP traffic with yorishiro-proxy. You can use either a manual browser setup or playwright-cli for automated capture.

docs.title: Step 1: Start the proxy
docs.text:
Ask Claude Code to start the proxy, or use the proxy_start tool directly:

// proxy_start
{
  "listen_addr": "127.0.0.1:8080"
}

The proxy is now listening on 127.0.0.1:8080.

docs.title: Step 2: Configure your browser
docs.text:
Set your browser or system HTTP proxy to http://127.0.0.1:8080. You can also set environment variables for command-line tools:

export HTTP_PROXY=http://127.0.0.1:8080
export HTTPS_PROXY=http://127.0.0.1:8080

docs.title: Step 3: Generate traffic
docs.text:
Browse to any website or make HTTP requests through the proxy. For a quick test:

curl -x http://127.0.0.1:8080 http://httpbin.org/get

For HTTPS (requires the CA certificate installed, or use -k to skip verification):

curl -x http://127.0.0.1:8080 -k https://httpbin.org/get

docs.title: Playwright-cli capture
docs.text: If you have playwright-cli installed, you can capture browser traffic without manual browser configuration.

docs.title: Step 1: Configure playwright-cli
docs.text:
Run install playwright to auto-detect your system browser and generate the configuration:

yorishiro-proxy install playwright

This command:

  • Auto-detects an installed browser (priority: chromium > firefox > chrome)
  • Generates .playwright/cli.config.json with the detected browser settings
  • Auto-installs the browser via npx playwright install if not found
  • Applies --no-sandbox automatically in container environments (Docker, Codespaces, Gitpod)

The generated configuration looks like this (values depend on your environment):

{
  "browser": {
    "browserName": "chromium",
    "launchOptions": {
      "channel": "chromium",
      "proxy": {
        "server": "http://127.0.0.1:8080"
      }
    },
    "contextOptions": {
      "ignoreHTTPSErrors": true
    }
  }
}

The ignoreHTTPSErrors: true option bypasses SSL certificate errors, so you do not need to install the CA certificate when using playwright-cli.

You can also create or edit this file manually if you need a specific browser or custom settings.

docs.title: Step 2: Start the proxy
docs.text:
// proxy_start
{
  "listen_addr": "127.0.0.1:8080"
}

docs.title: Step 3: Open a page
docs.text:
Use playwright-cli to open a browser that routes through the proxy:

playwright-cli open https://httpbin.org/get

All browser traffic flows through yorishiro-proxy and is recorded as flows.

docs.title: View captured flows
docs.text:
List all captured flows:

// query
{"resource": "flows"}

This returns all captured flows with their IDs, methods, URLs, status codes, and timestamps.

docs.title: Filter flows
docs.text:
To find specific requests, use the filter parameter:

// query
{
  "resource": "flows",
  "filter": {"url_pattern": "httpbin.org", "method": "GET"},
  "limit": 10
}

docs.title: Inspect request details
docs.text:
Drill into an individual flow to see the full request and response:

// query
{"resource": "flow", "id": "<flow-id>"}

This returns the complete request and response, including headers, body, status code, and timing information.

For streaming protocols (WebSocket, gRPC, HTTP/2), flows contain multiple messages. List them with:

// query
{
  "resource": "messages",
  "id": "<flow-id>",
  "limit": 50
}

docs.title: Resend a request
docs.text:
Replay a captured request as-is:

// resend_http
{
  "flow_id": "<flow-id>"
}

Or resend with modifications -- for example, changing a header:

// resend_http
{
  "flow_id": "<flow-id>",
  "headers": [
    {"name": "Authorization", "value": "Bearer <different-token>"}
  ]
}

To preview changes, modify the method and inspect the new stream after the call:

// resend_http
{
  "flow_id": "<flow-id>",
  "method": "PUT"
}

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
With the basic setup complete, explore these topics:

  • Resender -- advanced request replay and mutation
  • Fuzzer -- automated payload injection
  • Target scope -- control which traffic is captured
  • Intercept -- hold and modify requests in real time
  • Web UI -- visual interface for browsing flows and running tests

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: yorishiro-proxy is distributed as a single binary. You can install it from npm, download a pre-built release, or build from source.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Claude Code -- yorishiro-proxy operates as an MCP server for Claude Code
  • Node.js / npm -- required only if installing via npm
  • Go 1.25+ -- required only if building from source
  • playwright-cli (optional) -- for automated browser-based traffic capture

docs.title: Install via npm
docs.text:
The @usk6666/yorishiro-proxy package installs the prebuilt binary for your platform as an optional dependency. There is no postinstall script and no network fetch at install time, so it works with --ignore-scripts, in CI, and behind corporate proxies.

# Install globally
npm i -g @usk6666/yorishiro-proxy

# Or run without installing
npx @usk6666/yorishiro-proxy install

Supported platforms: Linux (x64, arm64), macOS (x64, arm64), and Windows (x64).

The npm distribution, GitHub Releases, and the yorishiro-proxy upgrade self-update path all coexist — use whichever fits your workflow.

docs.title: Download from GitHub Releases
docs.text:
Download the latest pre-built binary from the GitHub Releases page. Assets are named yorishiro-proxy-{version}-{os}-{arch} (e.g., yorishiro-proxy-v1.0.0-linux-amd64; Windows binaries have an .exe suffix).

macOS / LinuxWindows

Visit the Releases page and download the binary for your platform, or use curl:

# Replace VERSION, OS, and ARCH with your values.
# OS: linux, darwin  ARCH: amd64, arm64
curl -Lo yorishiro-proxy \
  "https://github.com/usk6666/yorishiro-proxy/releases/download/VERSION/yorishiro-proxy-VERSION-OS-ARCH"
chmod +x yorishiro-proxy
sudo mv yorishiro-proxy /usr/local/bin/

Download the .exe binary from the Releases page and place it in a directory on your PATH.

docs.title: Build from source
docs.text:
Clone the repository and build with make:

git clone https://github.com/usk6666/yorishiro-proxy.git
cd yorishiro-proxy
make build

This produces the binary at bin/yorishiro-proxy. Move it to a directory on your PATH:

sudo mv bin/yorishiro-proxy /usr/local/bin/

docs.title: Verify the installation
docs.text:
Run the help command to confirm the binary is working:

yorishiro-proxy -h

You should see the version, usage information, and available flags.

The binary also embeds its own reference documentation, which you can read without starting a server:

yorishiro-proxy docs                    # list every topic
yorishiro-proxy docs getting-started    # print a topic

See docs subcommand for details.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Quick setup -- one-command setup with yorishiro-proxy install
  • MCP configuration -- manual MCP client configuration

docs.title: MCP configuration
docs.text:
yorishiro-proxy runs as an MCP server. By default, it starts an HTTP MCP transport on a random loopback port. To use it with Claude Code via stdio transport, you need a .mcp.json file in your project root or home directory that launches the proxy with -stdio-mcp.

Tip

You can automate this setup by running yorishiro-proxy install (see Quick setup).

docs.title: Transport modes
docs.text:
yorishiro-proxy supports two MCP transport modes:

Mode Default Description HTTP MCP Enabled (127.0.0.1:0) Streamable HTTP transport + Web UI. The server writes connection details to ~/.yorishiro-proxy/server.json for automatic discovery Stdio MCP Disabled Stdin/stdout transport for direct integration with MCP clients like Claude Code

You can enable both transports simultaneously, or disable HTTP MCP for stdio-only mode.

docs.title: Manual configuration
docs.text:
Create a .mcp.json file in your project root with the following content:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "yorishiro-proxy": {
      "command": "/path/to/bin/yorishiro-proxy",
      "args": ["server", "-stdio-mcp", "-insecure", "-log-file", "/tmp/yorishiro-proxy.log"]
    }
  }
}

Replace /path/to/bin/yorishiro-proxy with the actual path to the binary. For example:

  • If built from source: "/home/user/yorishiro-proxy/bin/yorishiro-proxy"
  • If downloaded from GitHub Releases: "/usr/local/bin/yorishiro-proxy"

Note

The server subcommand and -stdio-mcp flag are required when launching from .mcp.json. Claude Code communicates over stdin/stdout, so stdio MCP must be explicitly enabled. The server subcommand is optional (it is the default), but including it makes the intent clear.

docs.title: CLI flags
docs.text:
Common flags to include in the args array:

Flag Default Description -stdio-mcp false Enable stdio MCP transport (required for Claude Code integration via .mcp.json) -no-http-mcp false Disable HTTP MCP transport (use with -stdio-mcp for stdio-only mode) -insecure false Skip upstream TLS certificate verification (useful for testing) -log-file <path> stderr Write logs to a file instead of stderr (keeps MCP stdio clean) -log-level <level> info Log verbosity: debug, info, warn, error -log-format <format> text Log format: text, json -db <name-or-path> ~/.yorishiro-proxy/yorishiro.db SQLite database path or project name -ca-ephemeral false Use an ephemeral in-memory CA (no persistent certificate files) -tls-fingerprint <profile> -- TLS fingerprint profile: chrome, firefox, safari, edge, random, none -config <path> -- JSON config file path for proxy defaults -mcp-http-addr <host:port> 127.0.0.1:0 Streamable HTTP listen address (also serves the Web UI) -mcp-http-token <token> auto-generated HTTP Bearer auth token for the Web UI -open-browser false Open WebUI in browser when HTTP MCP starts -target-policy-file <path> -- Target scope policy JSON file path -safety-filter false Enable SafetyFilter engine

The -db flag accepts an absolute path, a relative path with extension, or a plain project name. A project name (e.g., pentest-2026) resolves to ~/.yorishiro-proxy/pentest-2026.db, making it easy to maintain separate databases per engagement.

docs.title: Example with stdio + HTTP MCP
docs.text:
When both transports are active, Claude Code communicates via stdio while you can also access the Web UI and use the client subcommand:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "yorishiro-proxy": {
      "command": "/path/to/bin/yorishiro-proxy",
      "args": [
        "server",
        "-stdio-mcp",
        "-insecure",
        "-log-file", "/tmp/yorishiro-proxy.log",
        "-mcp-http-addr", "127.0.0.1:3000"
      ]
    }
  }
}

docs.title: Example with stdio only (no HTTP MCP)
docs.text:
To disable the HTTP MCP transport and use stdio only (similar to pre-v0.14.0 behavior):

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "yorishiro-proxy": {
      "command": "/path/to/bin/yorishiro-proxy",
      "args": [
        "server",
        "-stdio-mcp",
        "-no-http-mcp",
        "-insecure",
        "-log-file", "/tmp/yorishiro-proxy.log"
      ]
    }
  }
}

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text:
All flags accept environment variables with the YP_ prefix as a fallback. Replace hyphens with underscores and uppercase the name.

Flag Environment variable -db YP_DB -insecure YP_INSECURE -log-level YP_LOG_LEVEL -log-format YP_LOG_FORMAT -log-file YP_LOG_FILE -ca-cert YP_CA_CERT -ca-key YP_CA_KEY -ca-ephemeral YP_CA_EPHEMERAL -config YP_CONFIG -tls-fingerprint YP_TLS_FINGERPRINT -mcp-http-addr YP_MCP_HTTP_ADDR -mcp-http-token YP_MCP_HTTP_TOKEN -no-http-mcp YP_NO_HTTP_MCP -stdio-mcp YP_STDIO_MCP -open-browser YP_OPEN_BROWSER -target-policy-file YP_TARGET_POLICY_FILE -safety-filter YP_SAFETY_FILTER_ENABLED

Priority: CLI flag > environment variable > config file > default value.

For example, to skip TLS verification via environment variable:

YP_INSECURE=true yorishiro-proxy server

docs.title: Verify the connection
docs.text:
After creating .mcp.json, restart Claude Code. You should see eleven MCP tools become available:

Tool Description proxy_start Start the proxy listener proxy_stop Stop the proxy listener configure Change runtime settings (capture scope, intercept rules, TLS passthrough, etc.) query Retrieve flows, status, configuration, and fuzz results resend Resend captured requests with optional mutations fuzz Start, pause, resume, and cancel fuzz campaigns macro Define and run multi-step macro workflows intercept Release, modify, or drop intercepted requests manage Delete, export, and import flows security Configure target scope rules, rate limits, and budgets plugin List, reload, enable, and disable Starlark plugins

If the tools do not appear, check the log file for errors. Common issues include an incorrect binary path or permission problems.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:

  • First capture -- capture your first traffic
  • CLI flags -- full CLI flag reference

docs.title: Quick setup
docs.text: The yorishiro-proxy install command performs MCP configuration and CA certificate generation in a single step. This is the fastest way to get started.

docs.title: One-command setup
docs.text:
Run the install command to configure everything at once:

yorishiro-proxy install

This performs the following:

  1. Registers yorishiro-proxy as an MCP server in your project-level .mcp.json
  2. Generates the CA certificate for HTTPS interception

To also register the CA certificate in your OS trust store (requires sudo on macOS/Linux, or Administrator on Windows):

yorishiro-proxy install --trust

Vulnerability-verification playbooks ship over MCP

yorishiro-proxy used to copy a .claude/skills/yorishiro/ skill tree into your project as part of install. That tree is gone — the same playbooks are now delivered to your MCP host as MCP Prompts and become visible automatically the first time the host connects. No extra install step is required. The install skills subcommand and the --skills-dir flag have been removed.

docs.title: Individual setup targets
docs.text:
You can run specific setup targets independently:

Command Description yorishiro-proxy install mcp Configure MCP server integration only yorishiro-proxy install ca Generate the CA certificate only yorishiro-proxy install playwright Set up playwright-cli integration (auto-detects browser, installs if needed)

For example, to generate the CA certificate and register it in your OS trust store without touching MCP configuration:

yorishiro-proxy install ca --trust

docs.title: Additional flags
docs.text: Flag Description --trust Register the CA certificate in the OS trust store --interactive Launch a wizard that walks you through each step --user-scope Register MCP configuration in the user-level settings file (~/.claude/settings.json) instead of the project-level .mcp.json

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text:
Update yorishiro-proxy to the latest release from GitHub:

yorishiro-proxy upgrade

To check for updates without installing:

yorishiro-proxy upgrade --check

The bundled MCP prompts ship inside the binary, so a fresh yorishiro-proxy upgrade automatically delivers the latest playbook content the next time your MCP host reconnects — no separate install step is needed.
